source_file: 10762371_2025_Domonique Cornell Wilson, et al. v. Holiday Estates, et al._mied
case_name: Domonique Cornell Wilson, et al. v. Holiday Estates, et al.
text: The court summarily dismissed plaintiffs' federal Fair Housing Act and § 1983 claims for failure to state a claim because plaintiffs failed to allege discrimination or retaliation based on any protected category under the FHA and all defendants were private parties not subject to § 1983, then declined supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law claims. Plaintiff Wilson filed suit on behalf of himself and his minor children against his mobile home landlord Holiday Estates and related defendants, alleging that a gas leak and HVAC problems made his family ill, that he complained about these conditions, and that defendants retaliated by attempting to evict the family. The court granted in forma pauperis status but, after issuing a show cause order that plaintiffs failed to adequately answer, summarily dismissed all federal claims because plaintiffs had not alleged discrimination or retaliation tied to any protected category under the FHA, and because § 1983 does not apply to private parties. The court then declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state law negligence and emotional distress claims, dismissing them without prejudice. Plaintiff failed to allege that defendants discriminated or retaliated based on any protected category under the Fair Housing Act. The complaint alleges only a gas leak, HVAC problems, and retaliation for complaints about those conditions, which do not constitute FHA violations without a nexus to a protected class. Failure to state a claim § 1983 claims cannot proceed against private parties; state law claims dismissed without prejudice as supplemental jurisdiction was declined after all federal claims were dismissed. Failure to state a claim; lack of subject matter jurisdiction

source_file: 10766939_2025_Blakelick Properties, LLC v. The Village of Glen Ellyn_ilnd
case_name: Blakelick Properties, LLC v. The Village of Glen Ellyn
text: The Court granted preliminary injunction against Glen Ellyn's short-term rental ban as applied to Blakelick, finding Blakelick likely succeeded on its regulatory takings claim and would suffer irreparable harm from loss of its short-term rental business. Blakelick Properties LLC, owner of a short-term rental property in Glen Ellyn, Illinois, sued the Village of Glen Ellyn challenging Ordinance No. 7180-VC which bans short-term rentals, arguing it constitutes a regulatory taking under the Fifth Amendment. The Court granted preliminary injunction, finding Blakelick demonstrated likelihood of success on the merits of its regulatory taking claim, would suffer irreparable harm from loss of its entire short-term rental business, and the balance of equities favors enjoining enforcement against Blakelick while litigation proceeds. Court found Blakelick likely to succeed on the merits of its regulatory takings claim, that it would suffer irreparable harm without adequate legal remedy, and that the balance of equities favors Blakelick. The court granted a preliminary injunction against Glen Ellyn's enforcement of the short-term rental ban ordinance as to Blakelick only, finding the ordinance would deprive Blakelick of economically viable use of the property. Preliminary Injunction Granted The court noted that Blakelick alleged a Fair Housing Act violation but did not analyze the merits of this claim, instead focusing its preliminary injunction analysis on the regulatory takings claim. The FHA claim remains pending and unresolved. Not Reached

source_file: 10787023_2026_United States of America v. Douglas S. Waterbury, Carol A. Waterbury, E_A Management Co., and Ontario Realty, Inc._nynd
case_name: United States of America v. Douglas S. Waterbury, Carol A. Waterbury, E&A Management Co., and Ontario Realty, Inc.
text: The consent decree, which was entered on August 9, 2019 with a five-year effective period, expired on August 9, 2024, and neither party moved to extend it, so the case must be dismissed with prejudice. The United States government sued landlords and property management companies for Fair Housing Act violations, a consent decree was entered in 2019, and defendants were later held in contempt for violating it. On defendants' motion, the court dismissed the case with prejudice because the five-year consent decree expired on August 9, 2024, and neither party sought to extend it. The parties entered into a signed consent decree on August 9, 2019, which resolved the FHA claims without adjudication on the merits. The case was subsequently dismissed with prejudice on February 9, 2026, after the five-year term of the consent decree expired and neither party sought extension. Consent Decree

source_file: 10805225_2026_Elhadj Alpha Mahmound Souare v. Akron Metropolitan Housing Authority, et al._ohnd
case_name: Elhadj Alpha Mahmound Souare v. Akron Metropolitan Housing Authority, et al.
text: The federal district court lacks subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine to review a state court eviction judgment, and therefore dismissed plaintiff's complaint without addressing the merits of his Fair Housing Act claims. Plaintiff Elhadj Alpha Mahmound Souare sued Akron Metropolitan Housing Authority and Stephanie Pence in federal court, challenging his September 2024 eviction and raising Fair Housing Act claims. The federal court dismissed the complaint sua sponte for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, holding that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars federal district courts from reviewing state court judgments, and denied all pending motions as moot. The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's claims challenge a final state court eviction judgment, which only the U.S. Supreme Court may review. The complaint also cited 42 U.S.C. § 1983, the Fourteenth Amendment, and Ohio landlord-tenant law, but the court did not reach the merits of any claim. 12(b)(1)

source_file: 10808264_2026_Imani Lawson v. Dice Holdings LLC, Ozarks Communities, Theresa Knoth, and Daniel_ilsd
case_name: Imani Lawson v. Dice Holdings LLC, Ozarks Communities, Theresa Knoth, and Daniel
text: The court found it lacked subject matter jurisdiction because the plaintiff failed to allege membership in any protected class and failed to allege she engaged in protected activity under the FHA, and the Rooker-Feldman doctrine barred review of the underlying state court eviction judgment. Plaintiff Imani Lawson filed a complaint against her landlord/property management defendants seeking to vacate a state court eviction judgment, alleging Fair Housing Act violations including retaliation for disputing utility bills. The court found it lacked subject matter jurisdiction because the plaintiff failed to plead membership in any protected class or engagement in protected activity under the FHA, and Rooker-Feldman barred review of the state court judgment. The court found it lacked subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's alleged injuries (homelessness, property damage, emotional distress, financial hardship) resulted directly from the state court eviction judgment, and plaintiff explicitly sought to vacate that judgment. Additionally, plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class or engagement in protected FHA activity, failing to state a claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617. Jurisdictional dismissal under Rooker-Feldman and failure to state a claim

case_name: Steven Ray Collins; Sharon Lavette Collins v. Wells Fargo & Company; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.
text: The Ninth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claims against Wells Fargo as barred by res judicata, because the action involved the same cause of action between the same parties after a final judgment on the merits in a prior state court proceeding. Pro se plaintiffs Steven Ray Collins and Sharon Lavette Collins appealed the dismissal of their Fair Housing Act claims against Wells Fargo & Company and Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. The district court dismissed the action under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) on the ground that it was barred by res judicata, applying California's claim preclusion doctrine to give effect to a prior state court judgment involving the same cause of action and the same parties. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, also rejecting plaintiffs' procedural objections regarding the lack of oral argument and the alleged consideration of matters outside the pleadings. The appellate court affirmed the district court's dismissal under res judicata, holding that the FHA claims were barred by a prior final judgment on the merits in state court involving the same cause of action between the same parties under California law. 12(b)(6)

case_name: Group Home on Gibson Island v. Gibson Island Corp.
text: UNDETERMINED UNDETERMINED The court held that summary judgment was not appropriate because the plaintiff presented evidence that the defendant's litigation updates could have dissuaded a reasonable person from exercising FHA rights, creating a genuine dispute of material fact on whether the defendant's conduct was sufficiently adverse to constitute retaliation under § 3617. Rule 56

source_file: 3171091_2016_Richard Wolf v. Bank of America, N.A., et a_ca5
case_name: Richard B. Wolf; Marcia A. Wolf v. Bank of America National Association; Marvin Blankenship; Kianie King; Jimmy Widdle; Phil Gonzalez
text: The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal because the Wolfs failed to allege discriminatory intent or a significant discriminatory effect required to state a Fair Housing Act claim. Richard and Marcia Wolf sued Bank of America and several employees challenging the bank's refusal to refinance their residence and related foreclosure actions, asserting fraud, breach of contract, RICO, and Fair Housing Act claims. The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, finding the Wolfs' complaint failed to state a claim because they did not allege discriminatory intent or a significant discriminatory effect as required under the Fair Housing Act. The court affirmed dismissal of the FHA claim under the Iqbal/Twombly standard, finding that plaintiffs failed to allege either discriminatory intent or a significant discriminatory effect as required under 42 U.S.C. § 3604. The complaint's allegations regarding refinancing and note securitization do not plausibly state a discrimination claim based on a protected class. 12(b)(6) The court affirmed dismissal of fraud, breach of contract, and RICO claims under the Iqbal/Twombly standard. Plaintiffs failed to allege material misrepresentation (fraud), specific contractual breach or damages (breach of contract), or an enterprise and pattern of racketeering activity (RICO). 12(b)(6)

case_name: Kirschenbaum v. Assa Corp.
text: The Second Circuit affirmed that Assa Corporation, as Iran's alter ego and agency/instrumentality, is subject to the district court's jurisdiction and its property is subject to attachment and execution under both the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act and the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act. Hundreds of terrorism victims holding default judgments against Iran sought to attach assets of Assa Corporation (a New York corporation owned by Bank Melli, ultimately owned by the Government of Iran) under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act and Terrorism Risk Insurance Act. The Second Circuit affirmed, holding that Assa is Iran's alter ego as a matter of law and is therefore subject to the district court's jurisdiction, and that Assa's property constitutes blocked assets subject to attachment and execution under both statutes.

source_file: 4454484_2019_Daimeon Mosley v. Kohl's Dep't Stores, Inc._ca6
case_name: Daimeon Mosley v. Kohl's Department Stores, Inc.
text: The Sixth Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that Mosley established Article III standing to pursue his ADA Title III claim because he plausibly alleged intent to return to the Michigan stores based on his regular annual visits to family in the Detroit area and scheduled performances in southeast Michigan. Daimeon Mosley, a wheelchair user with disabilities including paralysis from West Nile Virus, sued Kohl's Department Stores under Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act alleging inaccessibility of restroom facilities at two Michigan stores. The district court dismissed for lack of standing, finding Mosley— who lives in Arizona and visited the stores only once—failed to allege a real and immediate threat of future injury. The Sixth Circuit reversed, holding that Mosley plausibly alleged standing based on his regular annual visits to the Detroit area to see family and scheduled performances, combined with his stated intent to return to the stores if made ADA-compliant. The district court dismissed for lack of standing under Article III, finding plaintiff failed to allege a real and immediate threat of future injury. The appellate court reversed, holding that plaintiff sufficiently alleged a plausible intent to return to the geographic area and interest in the accommodations based on his regular travel to Detroit, concrete plans to visit family and perform music, and statement that he would visit the stores if made ADA-compliant. The court remanded for further proceedings on the merits. 12(b)(1)

source_file: 4581562_2020_Dr. David S. Muransky v. Godiva Chocolatier, Inc._ca11
case_name: Dr. David S. Muransky v. Godiva Chocolatier, Inc.
text: The en banc Eleventh Circuit vacated the district court's approval of a class settlement, holding that the named plaintiff Dr. Muransky lacked Article III standing because he alleged only a bare statutory violation of FACTA without demonstrating concrete injury in fact as required by Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins. Dr. David Muransky filed a class action against Godiva Chocolatier alleging violations of FACTA for printing more than five digits of credit card numbers on receipts. The parties settled for $6.3 million, but objectors challenged the settlement arguing Muransky lacked Article III standing. The en banc Eleventh Circuit vacated the settlement approval, holding that Muransky failed to demonstrate concrete injury in fact beyond the bare statutory violation.

source_file: 4757512_2020_Akshar Global Investments Corp v. City of Los Angeles_ca9
case_name: Akshar Global Investments Corp. v. City of Los Angeles
text: The Ninth Circuit reversed dismissal of the Fourth Amendment Patel claim (related to warrantless searches of motel guest registration records) and remanded for leave to amend, while affirming dismissal of Fifth Amendment Takings, Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection, and Due Process claims. Akshar Global Investments Corp. and its owner Amitkumar Shah sued the City of Los Angeles under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act, challenging the revocation of the conditional use permit for their motel. The Ninth Circuit reversed the dismissal of the Fourth Amendment claim (regarding warrantless searches of guest registration records) for potential amendment, affirmed dismissal of takings, equal protection, and due process claims, and did not reach the FHA claim because it was not argued on appeal. The appellate court declined to address the FHA claim because appellants did not argue it in their opening brief, citing Miller v. Fairchild Industries for the rule that the Court of Appeals will not ordinarily consider matters on appeal that are not specifically and distinctly argued. Not addressed The court affirmed dismissal of most § 1983 claims for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly, finding that allegations were conclusory, lacked factual support, or failed to adequately allege a causal nexus between municipal policy and constitutional deprivation. The Fourth Amendment claim was reversed and remanded for amendment because appellants adequately alleged an official policy under Monell but failed to adequately allege the underlying Patel violation with sufficient specificity. Rule 12(b)(6)

source_file: 4768065_2020_Eric Ferrier v. Cascade Falls Condominium Association, Inc._ca11
case_name: Eric Ferrier v. Cascade Falls Condominium Association, Inc.
text: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal under Rooker-Feldman doctrine, holding that federal district courts lack subject matter jurisdiction over cases brought by state-court losers challenging state-court judgments rendered before the federal proceedings commenced. Eric Ferrier, proceeding pro se, appealed the district court's dismissal of his civil action challenging state foreclosure proceedings on his condominium; the Eleventh Circuit affirmed the dismissal, holding that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine barred federal subject matter jurisdiction because Ferrier was a state-court loser challenging injuries caused by state-court foreclosure judgments. The district court lacked subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because Ferrier was a state-court loser complaining of injuries caused by state-court foreclosure judgments rendered before the federal action commenced, and the relief requested invited district court review and rejection of those state judgments. The appellate court affirmed the jurisdictional dismissal without reaching the merits of any FHA claim. Rooker-Feldman jurisdictional dismissal All non-FHA claims were dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Rooker-Feldman. The court declined to recognize a fraud exception to the doctrine, holding that such an exception would effectively nullify the doctrine by permitting litigants to challenge state-court judgments in federal court merely by alleging fraud. Rooker-Feldman jurisdictional dismissal

case_name: Ricky Kamdem-Ouaffo v. Plaza Square Apartments
text: The Third Circuit affirmed the District Court's denial of an extension of time to file an amended complaint because Appellant failed to articulate any viable justification for reopening the case—he missed the deadline to amend, forfeited his FHA claim on a prior appeal by failing to brief it, and provided no indication that an amended complaint would cure the defects identified by the District Court. Ricky Kamdem-Ouaffo, proceeding pro se, appealed the District Court's denial of his motion for an extension of time to file an amended complaint in his Fair Housing Act case against Plaza Square Apartments. The Third Circuit affirmed, holding that Appellant provided no viable justification for reopening the case after missing the deadline to amend and forfeiting his FHA claim on a prior appeal by failing to brief it. The District Court dismissed the FHA claim for failure to meet pleading standards under Rule 8(a)(2), finding the complaint completely devoid of factual allegations supporting a discrimination claim. The Third Circuit affirmed, noting Appellant waived the FHA claim by failing to address it in appellate briefing and later forfeited his opportunity to amend by not filing a timely amended complaint and failing to articulate viable justification for Rule 60(b) relief. Rule 60(b) motion denied; affirmed on appeal Because the FHA claim was dismissed, the District Court properly dismissed the pendent state-law claims as well, and the Third Circuit affirmed this dismissal. Dismissed as pendent claims

source_file: 4886973_2021_Paul Clark, Sr. v. Council of Unit Owners_ca4
case_name: Paul C. Clark, Sr. v. Council of Unit Owners of the 100 Harborview Drive Condominium
text: The Fourth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of the Creditors' appeal as equitably moot and affirmed the bankruptcy court's damages award to the Creditors, rejecting the Creditors' arguments regarding their FHA claims which had been disposed of at summary judgment. Paul C. Clark, Sr. and family members (Creditors) appealed to the Fourth Circuit from a district court ruling that had dismissed their bankruptcy appeal as equitably moot and affirmed a damages award against the Council of Unit Owners of the 100 Harborview Drive Condominium for property damage to the Creditors' penthouse unit. The Fourth Circuit affirmed, upholding the dismissal of the Creditors' appeal as equitably moot and the affirmation of the damages award, with the FHA claims having been resolved against the Creditors at summary judgment in the bankruptcy proceedings. The bankruptcy court awarded summary judgment to the Council on the Creditors' FHA claims. The district court affirmed the bankruptcy court's damages award on non-FHA breach of contract/property maintenance grounds. The appellate court affirmed the district court's dismissal of the Creditors' appeal as equitably moot, finding no reversible error in the bankruptcy court's legal conclusions or factual findings. Summary Judgment (FHA claims); Affirmed on appeal

case_name: Curtis Lockey, Jr. v. Marcia L. Fudge, Secretary, U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
text: The court dismissed the case as duplicative of Lockey's still-pending action in the Northern District of Texas, which had been stayed but not dismissed, and found the Northern District was the more appropriate forum based on local interest and judicial economy. Curtis Lockey, Jr., a developer who previously sued HUD and DOJ over alleged fair housing violations related to a failed Dallas low-income housing project, filed this duplicative action in the District of Columbia while a similar case remained pending in the Northern District of Texas. The court granted the government's motion to dismiss, finding the Northern District action was stayed but not closed, making this case an impermissible duplicate that should be adjudicated in Texas. The court dismissed the case as duplicative of a pending action in the Northern District of Texas under the doctrine of comity and judicial economy, finding that the Northern District was the more appropriate forum. The court did not reach the merits of the FHA claim because it exercised discretion to dismiss based on parallel pending litigation involving the same parties and nearly identical claims. Duplicative Litigation / Discretionary Dismissal

case_name: Nicole Fedynich; Elizabeth Fedynich v. Juana Lozano; Marie White; Steve Boyce; Angelica Redfern; Valor Phase II, LP; S.L. Nusbaum Realty, Co.
text: The Fourth Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction because the district court's dismissal order was not final — one retaliation claim under the Fair Housing Act remains pending before the district court. Nicole and Elizabeth Fedynich, proceeding pro se, appealed the district court's dismissal of seven of their eight claims against apartment management defendants, while a retaliation claim under the Fair Housing Act remained pending below. The Fourth Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that the district court order was not final because it did not resolve all claims as to all parties. The appellate court lacked jurisdiction to hear the appeal because the reasonable accommodation claim was still pending before the district court, meaning the district court's order dismissing seven of eight claims was not final. Dismissed for lack of jurisdiction The retaliation claim remained pending before the district court, preventing the appellate court from exercising jurisdiction over the appeal of the dismissal orders. Pending before district court

source_file: 6225633_2022_Karen C. Yeh Ho v. Valencia Isles Homeowners Association, Inc._ca11
case_name: Karen C. Yeh Ho v. Valencia Isles Homeowners Association, Inc.
text: The district court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing the complaint without prejudice for failure to timely respond to the motion to dismiss, where the plaintiff continued to file other documents and was properly warned of potential dismissal. Pro se plaintiff Karen Yeh-Ho appealed the dismissal without prejudice of her Fair Housing Act complaint against Valencia Isles Homeowners Association and related defendants; the Eleventh Circuit affirmed, holding the district court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing the complaint for the plaintiff's failure to timely respond to the motion to dismiss despite continued filings and proper notice. The district court dismissed the complaint for failure to timely respond to the motion to dismiss and failure to cure the default despite explicit warning. The appellate court affirmed under abuse of discretion review, finding no clear error in the district court's procedural dismissal. The merits of the FHA claim were never reached. Affirmed dismissal without prejudice The district court dismissed the complaint for failure to timely respond to the motion to dismiss and failure to cure the default despite explicit warning. The appellate court affirmed under abuse of discretion review, finding no clear error in the district court's procedural dismissal. The merits of the FHA retaliation claim were never reached. Affirmed dismissal without prejudice

source_file: 6472707_2022_Commissiong v. US Dept. Housing _ Urban Development_ca2
case_name: Commissiong v. US Dept. Housing & Urban Development
text: The court affirmed dismissal based on sovereign immunity, holding that HUD and its officials are immune from suit under the FHA and that Commissiong failed to identify a valid waiver of sovereign immunity. Carol Commissiong filed a HUD administrative complaint alleging housing discrimination in violation of the FHA regarding her apartment; after HUD issued a finding of no reasonable cause, she filed an Article 78 petition against HUD and HUD employees in state court. The court affirmed dismissal, holding that sovereign immunity bars suit against HUD and its officials because the FHA does not create a private right of action against federal agencies and Commissiong failed to identify any valid waiver of sovereign immunity. The court affirmed dismissal on jurisdictional grounds, holding that the FHA does not create a private right of action against HUD and HUD officials, and that HUD and federal officers are protected by sovereign immunity absent an unequivocal waiver. The plaintiff bore the burden of establishing a waiver and failed to do so. 12(b)(1)

source_file: 8509670_2022_Sandpiper Residents Association v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development_dcd
case_name: Sandpiper Residents Association v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
text: The court denied plaintiffs' Rule 59(e) motion for reconsideration because the sale of the property to a new owner rendered all claims moot—the statutory precondition for issuing Tenant Protection Vouchers (a Notice of Default against the current owner) was no longer satisfied. Sandpiper Cove tenants and the Sandpiper Residents Association sued HUD seeking an order requiring HUD to issue Tenant Protection Vouchers due to substandard housing conditions at the PBRA-subsidized complex. The court denied plaintiffs' motion to reconsider its prior dismissal on mootness grounds, holding that because the property was sold to a new owner who had not received a Notice of Default, the statutory prerequisite for issuing vouchers was no longer satisfied. The court dismissed the FHA claim as moot because the property was sold to a new owner who had not received a Notice of Default, eliminating the statutory prerequisite for issuing Tenant Protection Vouchers. The court lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate the claim and therefore did not reach the merits of the FHA theory. Mootness/Jurisdictional The court dismissed all non-FHA claims (APA and Fifth Amendment equal protection) as moot on the same jurisdictional basis: the sale of the property to a new owner eliminated the statutory prerequisites for relief, depriving the court of jurisdiction to adjudicate any claim. Mootness/Jurisdictional

case_name: Chris Langer v. Milan Kiser
text: A place of public accommodation violates Title III of the ADA by opening its parking lot to customers without disabilities without providing accessible van-accessible parking spaces, and district courts cannot use a plaintiff's extensive ADA litigation history to undermine their credibility or intent to return. Chris Langer, a paraplegic who uses a wheelchair and drives a van with a side-deploying ramp, sued property owners Milan and Diana Kiser under Title III of the ADA, alleging their commercial property's parking lot lacked required van-accessible parking spaces, preventing him from accessing businesses on the property. The Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's judgment for the defendants, holding that (1) the parking lot was a facility of a place of public accommodation because customers of the Lobster Shop actually used it regardless of lease terms, (2) Langer had Article III standing as a serial litigant with tester standing, and (3) the district court improperly relied on Langer's litigation history to discredit his testimony about intent to return. Appellate court reversed district court's judgment on Title III ADA claim, holding that the parking lot was a facility of a place of public accommodation (the Lobster Shop) subject to ADA requirements, and that actual usage—not lease terms—controls whether a facility is open to the public. Overwhelming trial evidence showed customers parked in the lot, establishing ADA violation. Court also rejected district court's adverse credibility determination against serial litigant plaintiff as based on impermissible legal reasoning under CREEC and D'Lil precedent. Reversed and remanded

source_file: 9402431_2023_Joelle Angel v. Charlestowne Condominium Association, Inc._ca4
case_name: Angel v. Charlestowne Condominium Association, Inc.
text: The Fourth Circuit affirmed the district court's order remanding the case to state court for lack of federal subject matter jurisdiction, finding no reversible error in the procedural ruling. Multiple individual unit owners appealed a district court order remanding their removed action to state court for lack of federal subject matter jurisdiction and denying their sanctions motions against the Charlestowne Condominium Association. The Fourth Circuit found jurisdiction to review the remand based on the § 1443 removal statute but affirmed on the merits, with the substantive FHA claims remaining unresolved. District court remanded the action to state court for lack of federal subject matter jurisdiction. The appellate court affirmed the remand order, finding no reversible error. The opinion does not address the merits of the FHA counterclaim, only the jurisdictional basis for removal under 28 U.S.C. § 1443. Remand to state court

case_name: James Nathaniel Douse v. Sabrina Traeger
text: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal because plaintiff's FHA complaint was wholly insubstantial and frivolous, containing no factual allegations establishing a violation of any FHA provision, and even construing the complaint generously, the claims regarding HOA fees and property deposits did not relate to discriminatory conduct on a protected basis. James Douse, proceeding pro se, appealed the sua sponte dismissal of his Fair Housing Act complaint against private individuals and a homeowners association for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, finding Douse's complaint wholly insubstantial and frivolous because it failed to allege any factual content establishing that defendants engaged in conduct prohibited by the FHA, instead raising only contract claims regarding HOA assessments and a pool construction deposit. The appellate court affirmed the district court's sua sponte dismissal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff's complaint failed to allege any factual allegations under the FHA count and did not relate to the sale or rental of a dwelling. The court found the FHA claims wholly insubstantial and frivolous, and plaintiff did not allege discriminatory conduct based on a protected class. Jurisdictional dismissal (28 U.S.C. § 1331)

case_name: Orlando Garcia v. Gateway Hotel L.P.
text: The ADA's fee- and cost-shifting provision (42 U.S.C. § 12205) does not 'provide otherwise' than Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(d)(1), and therefore a prevailing ADA defendant may be awarded costs at the district court's discretion without a finding that the plaintiff's action was frivolous, unreasonable, or without foundation. Orlando Garcia sued Gateway Hotel L.P. under the Americans with Disabilities Act, challenging the hotel's reservation policies and website practices regarding accessible rooms. After the district court dismissed the case and awarded costs to Gateway, Garcia appealed arguing ADA defendants should only receive costs if the action was frivolous. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that 42 U.S.C. § 12205 does not limit Rule 54(d)(1)'s discretionary cost award standard, effectively overruling prior precedent in Brown, and concluding the district court properly exercised discretion in awarding costs to the prevailing defendant. The appellate court affirmed the district court's award of costs to the prevailing ADA defendant under Rule 54(d)(1), holding that the ADA's fee- and cost-shifting provision (42 U.S.C. § 12205) does not 'provide otherwise' and thus does not displace Rule 54(d)(1)'s discretionary cost-award standard. The court held that Marx v. General Revenue Corp. effectively overruled Brown v. Lucky Stores, Inc., which had applied the Christiansburg standard to ADA cost awards. Rule 54(d)(1)

source_file: 9428257_2023_Sonya Youvett McNeal v. Navy Federal Credit Union_ca11
case_name: Sonya Youvett McNeal v. Navy Federal Credit Union
text: The Eleventh Circuit lacked jurisdiction to review the district court's dismissal of the complaint and denial of preliminary injunction due to procedural defects (untimely appeal and mootness), and affirmed the denial of the motion to recuse and first motion to reconsider on the merits. Sonya McNeal, proceeding pro se, appealed from a district court dismissal of her suit against Navy Federal Credit Union over a foreclosure dispute, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, CARES Act, and Due Process Clause. The Eleventh Circuit dismissed for lack of jurisdiction over the dismissal order (untimely appeal) and preliminary injunction denial (mootness), and affirmed the denial of the motion to recuse and first motion to reconsider. Plaintiff failed to timely appeal the district court's dismissal of her complaint within 30 days; subsequent motions to reconsider filed six months later did not toll the appeal deadline. The appellate court lacked jurisdiction to review the underlying dismissal order. Jurisdictional dismissal; no timely appeal of underlying MTD ruling

case_name: Amia L. Bryant v. Darrell Steinburg
text: The Ninth Circuit affirmed the dismissal because Bryant failed to allege facts sufficient to show that defendants discriminated against her on the basis of a protected status under 42 U.S.C. § 3604, lacking either allegations of intentional discrimination because of a protected characteristic or a discriminatory effect on a protected class. Amia L. Bryant, proceeding pro se, appealed the district court's dismissal of her Fair Housing Act claims against the Mayor of Sacramento, Sacramento Housing and Redevelopment Agency officials, and others in connection with a government housing program. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that Bryant failed to plead facts sufficient to establish either intentional discrimination because of a protected characteristic or a discriminatory effect on a protected class under 42 U.S.C. § 3604. District court properly dismissed FHA claims under § 1915(e)(2) because plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to show defendants discriminated against her on the basis of a protected status as required by 42 U.S.C. § 3604. The complaint did not establish either intentional discrimination because of a protected characteristic or a discriminatory effect on a protected class. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)

case_name: Victorio Campos v. 1169 Palms LLC
text: The court issued an order to show cause why it should not decline supplemental jurisdiction over plaintiff's state law claims because they substantially predominate over the Fair Housing Act and Civil Rights Act claims over which the court has original jurisdiction. Plaintiff Victorio Campos filed a First Amended Complaint against 1169 Palms LLC and related defendants alleging Fair Housing Act, California Fair Employment and Housing Act, and numerous state law claims. The court issued an order to show cause why it should not decline to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state law claims, finding they appear to substantially predominate over the federal claims. Court issued an Order to Show Cause regarding supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims, finding that plaintiff's state law claims substantially predominate over the FHA claim. The FHA claim itself was not addressed on the merits; the opinion concerns only jurisdictional analysis under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c). Order to Show Cause

source_file: 9516404_2023_Wilmington Savings Fund Society, FSB v. Bersadeh Bagheri_cacd
case_name: Wilmington Savings Fund Society, FSB v. Bersadeh Bagheri
text: The court granted plaintiff's motion to remand because defendant failed to establish federal question jurisdiction—the CARES Act, FHA, and PTFA were raised as potential defenses, not as basis for plaintiff's state-law unlawful detainer claim. Plaintiff Wilmington Savings Fund Society filed an unlawful detainer action in Los Angeles Superior Court against defendants including VRG, who removed the case to federal court arguing federal question jurisdiction based on the CARES Act, Fair Housing Act, and PTFA. The district court granted the motion to remand, finding no federal question jurisdiction because defendant raised these federal statutes as defenses rather than as basis for plaintiff's complaint. The court held that defendant's allegation of FHA violation constitutes a potential defense or counterclaim, not a federal question presented on the face of plaintiff's properly pleaded complaint. Under the well-pleaded complaint rule and Caterpillar, federal law defenses do not confer federal question jurisdiction, and the court remanded for lack of subject matter jurisdiction without reaching the merits of any FHA claim. Remand (12(b)(1) — lack of subject matter jurisdiction)

case_name: Arkansas United v. Thurston
text: The six-voter limit in Arkansas Code § 7-5-310(b)(4)(B) is preempted by Section 208 of the Voting Rights Act because it conflicts with the federal right of voters who require assistance to select any person of their choice as an assistor; however, the assistor-tracking requirement in § 7-5-310(b)(5) is not preempted because it does not prevent voters from selecting their assistor of choice. Arkansas United (an immigrant advocacy nonprofit) and its executive director sued Arkansas's Secretary of State and county election commissioners, alleging that Arkansas's six-voter limit for poll assistance conflicts with Section 208 of the Voting Rights Act. The federal district court granted partial summary judgment, holding that the six-voter limit is preempted by federal law because it impermissibly restricts voters who need assistance due to blindness, disability, or inability to read or write from selecting any person of their choice as an assistor, but upheld the state's separate tracking requirement as permissible.

case_name: Arkansas United and L. Mireya Reith v. John Thurston
text: The six-voter limit at Arkansas Code § 7-5-310(b)(4)(B) conflicts with Section 208 of the Voting Rights Act and is preempted, as it impermissibly narrows the right of voters requiring assistance to select the assistor of their choice. Arkansas United and its founder sued Arkansas state and county election officials, challenging the state's six-voter limit on ballot assistors as conflicting with Section 208 of the Voting Rights Act. The court granted partial summary judgment for plaintiffs, declaring the six-voter limit preempted and permanently enjoining its enforcement, while upholding the assistor-tracking requirement.

case_name: Project Sentinel v. Jeanette Komar
text: The court grants plaintiff's motion to correct the default judgment to properly name defendant Jeanette Komar and incorporate injunctive relief terms, but denies plaintiff's untimely request to add post-judgment interest. Project Sentinel, a fair housing nonprofit organization, obtained a default judgment against landlord Jeanette Komar for Fair Housing Act violations and now seeks to correct that judgment. The court grants the correction to properly reflect the defendant and incorporate injunctive relief terms but denies the untimely request to add post-judgment interest. This opinion addresses only procedural correction of a default judgment previously entered on June 4, 2021. The court granted plaintiff's motion to correct the judgment to reflect the correct defendant (Jeanette Komar only, not Sarah Komar) and to incorporate the terms of relief previously ordered, but denied the request to add post-judgment interest. The underlying FHA claims were resolved by default judgment, not addressed substantively in this opinion. Rule 60(a) correction of default judgment

case_name: Susan Marie Shultz v. Kern County, et al.
text: The court found that plaintiff's complaint failed to state a Fair Housing Act claim because she did not allege membership in a protected class or that she was treated differently because of her protected class status, and ordered her to file an amended complaint within 30 days or face dismissal. Pro se plaintiff Susan Shultz filed an IFP complaint against Kern County entities alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act after the sheriff's department allegedly vacated her from her rental apartment without notice in April 2020, leaving her unhoused and subsequently charged with trespassing. The court screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2) and concluded it failed to state an FHA claim because plaintiff did not allege she belonged to a protected class or that any differential treatment was due to her protected class status. The court granted leave to amend within 30 days, warning that failure to comply may result in a recommendation of dismissal. Plaintiff failed to allege facts establishing membership in a protected class (race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin) or that she was treated differently because of such status. The complaint does not state a plausible FHA disparate treatment claim under Iqbal/Twombly. Failure to State a Claim Without a viable federal FHA claim, the court lacks subject matter jurisdiction over state law claims. State housing law violations cannot form the basis of a federal lawsuit absent an independent federal question. Failure to State a Claim

case_name: Goodwin v. City Attorney's Office
text: Plaintiff's complaint was dismissed for failure to state a cognizable claim because it lacked any factual allegations identifying what happened, when it occurred, who was involved, and how any Fair Housing Act violation occurred. Pro se plaintiff Duchun Lafre Goodwin sued the City Attorney's Office under the Fair Housing Act, claiming intentional discrimination, but the case was dismissed at screening because the complaint lacked any factual allegations and failed to comply with the court's order to amend. The complaint was a barebones form that identified no specific housing transaction, no protected class basis with factual support, and no defendants' specific conduct. Plaintiff's complaint contains no factual allegations identifying what happened, when it happened, or who was involved, and fails to plausibly allege the prima facie elements of a Fair Housing Act disparate treatment claim under § 3604(a), including membership in a protected class, denial of housing, and that protected class was a motivating factor. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)

source_file: 9604396_2022_National Fair Housing Alliance, Inc. v. Carson_cand
case_name: National Fair Housing Alliance, et al. v. Marcia L. Fudge, et al.
text: The court granted the parties' joint request to stay proceedings for 90 days to allow HUD to complete its review of the discriminatory effects rule challenged in the APA complaint. Fair housing organizations sued HUD challenging a 2020 HUD rule on the Fair Housing Act's disparate impact standard as arbitrary and capricious under the APA. The court granted the parties' joint request to stay proceedings for 90 days to allow HUD to complete its ongoing review of the discriminatory effects rule following a Presidential Memorandum directing HUD to examine the rule's effects.

case_name: Rex A. Frederickson v. Dustin Kenneth, Larimer County (Code Compliance), Chad Grey, Michael J. Weiss, and Other Unknown Actors or Conspirators
text: The Court granted the motion to dismiss because the Plaintiff's objections to the Magistrate Judge's recommendation were not specific enough to meet the requirements of Fed. R. Civ. P. 72(b)(3), consisting largely of general legal recitations without explaining how they applied to the case. Pro se plaintiff Rex A. Frederickson sued Larimer County code compliance officials and other defendants, and the Magistrate Judge recommended granting defendants' motion to dismiss. The district court overruled the plaintiff's objection, affirmed the recommendation, and granted the motion to dismiss because the plaintiff's objections were not specific and failed to adequately address the Magistrate Judge's thorough analysis. Plaintiff's complaint failed to state plausible claims under the Iqbal/Twombly standard. The allegations were too general and conclusory, lacking specific factual content to support liability. Plaintiff failed to allege any specific custom, policy, or practice supporting Monell liability against Larimer County. 12(b)(6)

case_name: Alexander McArthur v. Nur Market
text: The complaint fails to state a federal claim because plaintiff has not alleged an employment relationship with the defendant (Title VII), has not demonstrated nexus to housing (FHA § 3617), and cannot proceed on unrelated state law or criminal statutes Alexander McArthur sued Nur Market, a grocery store, alleging that a store clerk overcharged him for merchandise; the court dismissed the complaint for failure to state any cognizable federal claim, including Title VII, public accommodation discrimination under § 2000a, and Fair Housing Act claims under § 3617, declining to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims. Court dismissed the § 3617 claim because plaintiff alleged no facts with any nexus to housing and did not allege interference with rights protected by the Fair Housing Act, which applies only to housing-related transactions enumerated in §§ 3603-3606. Dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)

case_name: Morales v. U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
text: HUD's claims dismissed due to sovereign immunity and lack of waiver; HACH's claims dismissed for failure to allege sufficient facts to state plausible claims of discrimination or retaliation under Title VI and the FHA Angel Morales sued HUD and Hartford Housing Authority alleging discrimination in violation of Title VI and the Fair Housing Act, claiming HACH improperly refused to let him purchase a house that his family had rented since 1999. The court granted both motions to dismiss, finding HUD immune from suit under sovereign immunity and that Morales failed to state plausible claims against HACH due to sparse factual allegations. Complaint fails to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly because it contains only threadbare allegations and does not allege facts from which the court could infer discrimination based on membership in a protected class. Plaintiff failed to identify any protected class basis for the alleged discrimination. 12(b)(6) Complaint fails to allege facts suggesting coercion, intimidation, threatening, or interference with FHA rights under 42 U.S.C. § 3617. Allegations are conclusory and lack factual detail necessary to state a plausible retaliation claim. 12(b)(6) Claims against HUD dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction based on sovereign immunity. HUD, as a federal agency, is shielded by sovereign immunity, and plaintiff failed to identify an applicable waiver of sovereign immunity under the Civil Rights Acts or the APA. Dismissal without prejudice as to Title VI claim to allow plaintiff to challenge HUD's Title VI compliance determination under the APA. 12(b)(1)

case_name: Earlando Samuel v. Robert Rizzo, et al.
text: The court dismissed plaintiff's retaliation and interference claims under § 3617 because his factual allegations failed to meet the required standards—NCCHA's document requests were permissible regulatory actions, the inspection timing complied with biennial requirements, and the isolated instances of service providers entering his apartment did not rise to the level of actionable harassment or interference. Earlando Samuel, a pro se plaintiff who rented an apartment with Section 8 assistance, sued New Castle County Housing Authority, Fairville Management Company, and Greenlawn Apartments alleging harassment and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act for complaining about unsafe housing conditions. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss and for judgment on the pleadings, finding Samuel's factual allegations failed to state actionable retaliation or interference claims under 42 U.S.C. § 3617. Plaintiff's allegations against NCCHA Defendants fail to state a plausible § 3617 retaliation claim because: (1) requesting bank statements and raising rent in response to non-compliance are not retaliatory acts—they are authorized regulatory actions; (2) failure to provide documents is not a protected activity; (3) biennial inspection schedule was compliant with regulations; and (4) alleged deficiencies existed in prior inspections, breaking any causal link between complaints and adverse actions. 12(b)(6) Plaintiff's allegations against Greenlawn Defendants and Fairville Management Company fail to state a plausible § 3617 interference claim. Requesting renters' insurance after water damage is reasonable and not retaliatory (same request made to similarly situated neighbor). Service providers entering apartment for scheduled appointments, while potentially questionable under state law, does not rise to the level of severe or pervasive interference required under § 3617, as distinguished by case law involving sustained harassment campaigns. 12(c)

source_file: 9636368_2023_Lewis v. Greenville on 141 Apartments and Townhomes - Westover Companies_ded
case_name: Racquel Lewis v. Greenville on 141 Apartments and Townhomes — Westover Companies
text: The complaint was dismissed because plaintiff failed to state a claim under the Fair Housing Act, having alleged precious few factual allegations with specificity and relying on inapplicable Washington D.C. municipal laws. Pro se plaintiff Racquel Lewis filed suit against her apartment complex owner alleging Fair Housing Act violations related to rental assistance payments from DEHAP and an attempted eviction. The Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding plaintiff failed to plead sufficient factual allegations and relied on inapplicable Washington D.C. laws, but granted leave to amend. Court dismissed for failure to state a claim under the Iqbal/Twombly standard, finding it unclear under which FHA provisions plaintiff was attempting to bring her claims and that she alleged precious few factual allegations with specificity. Plaintiff was granted leave to file an amended complaint. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)

case_name: James Nathaniel Douse v. Sabrina Traeger, et al.
text: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims were dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because he failed to identify his membership in any protected class (race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, or national origin) and failed to describe any discriminatory conduct covered under the FHA. Pro se plaintiff James Douse sued his homeowners association and an employee over a disputed pool construction deposit and assessment charges, vaguely referencing the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed the case for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding the FHA claims were wholly insubstantial because plaintiff failed to identify his membership in any protected class or allege discriminatory conduct covered under the statute. Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to identify any protected class status (race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, or national origin) and the conduct complained of (pool deposit delay and assessment misclassification) does not fit within any prohibited discrimination enumerated in § 3604. The FHA claims are wholly insubstantial and frivolous, insufficient to confer federal question jurisdiction. 12(b)(1)

case_name: Josephine Guion v. Bonner Homeless Transitions Board of Directors
text: The court denied Guion's motion to vacate summary judgment because she failed to establish fraud on the court by clear and convincing evidence, as her allegations consisted of legal challenges to the court's prior conclusions rather than actual evidence of fraud, and a mere misstatement of a date does not constitute fraud on the court. Josephine Guion moved to vacate the court's prior summary judgment ruling dismissing her Fair Housing Act claims, alleging fraud on the court, and also moved to disqualify the presiding judge and for an indicative ruling under Rule 62.1. The court denied all three motions, finding that Guion failed to establish fraud on the court by clear and convincing evidence and that her allegations were merely legal challenges to the court's prior conclusions rather than evidence of an unconscionable scheme to improperly influence the court. The court dismissed the FHA claim on summary judgment primarily on statute of limitations grounds under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A) (two-year limitations period), with the court noting that even setting aside statute of limitations issues, the claims would have been dismissed due to substantive deficiencies. The court did not reach the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim itself. Rule 56 The fraud claim was dismissed on substantive grounds (not statute of limitations). The court found no evidence of fraud on the court by clear and convincing evidence, as required under Rule 60(d)(3) and Ninth Circuit precedent. Rule 56

case_name: James Alan Gerdon v. Reynold French
text: The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss without prejudice because plaintiff's complaint failed to establish federal jurisdiction, did not state a cognizable Fair Housing Act claim (42 U.S.C. § 3631 was inapplicable as no housing discrimination was alleged), and failed to state a plausible § 1983 claim for violation of constitutional rights; plaintiff was given leave to amend within 30 days. Pro se plaintiff James Gerdon sued probation officer Reynold French under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and various criminal statutes, alleging the officer came to his home with guns, used threats and physical force, and took his property while persecuting him for being an 'alternative lifestyle person.' The court granted French's motion to dismiss without prejudice, finding Gerdon failed to establish federal jurisdiction, failed to state a viable FHA claim, and failed to allege a plausible constitutional violation under § 1983, though granting leave to amend. Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because criminal statutes cited do not provide private right of action, and plaintiff failed to allege facts establishing Fair Housing Act discrimination. Court also found no cognizable federal constitutional claim under § 1983 and improper service if suit was in official capacity. 12(b)(1), 12(b)(6)

case_name: Richard Johnson v. Barry Flannery
text: Plaintiff failed to state a retaliation claim under § 3617 because reporting housing code violations to a health department is not a protected activity under the Fair Housing Act; plaintiff's allegations about being called racial slurs do not save the claim because retaliation focuses on what the plaintiff did, not who he is. Richard Johnson, a white tenant, sued his landlord Barry Flannery alleging retaliation under the Fair Housing Act for reporting building code and health violations to a government agency. The court dismissed the case with prejudice, finding that Johnson failed to state a viable retaliation claim because reporting housing code violations to a health department is not a protected activity under the FHA, and Johnson's allegations about being called racial slurs do not constitute protected activity under the retaliation provision. Plaintiff alleged retaliation under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 for reporting landlord to health department for failure to make repairs. Court held that reporting housing code violations to a government agency is not a protected activity under the Fair Housing Act (which protects only those exercising rights under §§ 3603-3606 related to discrimination based on protected class). Therefore, the alleged retaliation is not cognizable under the FHA's anti-retaliation provision, and the complaint fails to state a claim. Dismissal with prejudice

case_name: Nathaniel Satterfield, Jr. v. HSBC Bank USA, N.A., Wilmington Savings Fund Society FSB, Victor Vita, and Carrington Mortgage Services LLC
text: The court lacks subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because Satterfield's alleged injuries—loss of his home, failure to maintain the property, and failure to pay property taxes—were completed only when the state court ordered eviction, making his FHA claim not independent of the state court judgment; moreover, Satterfield had a reasonable opportunity to raise his FHA claims as equitable defenses in the state court eviction proceedings. Nathaniel Satterfield sued HSBC Bank USA, N.A. and related defendants alleging they wrongfully obtained possession of his home through meritless state court eviction proceedings and violated the Fair Housing Act by intimidating him using the threat of unlawful eviction. The court dismissed the case for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, holding that Satterfield's claimed injuries arose directly from the state court eviction orders and his FHA claim was therefore not independent of those judgments, and that he had a reasonable opportunity to raise his civil rights claims as defenses in the state eviction proceedings. The FHA interference/coercion claim is barred by the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's alleged injuries (loss of house, failure to maintain property, failure to pay taxes) were complete only when the state court ordered the eviction. The claim is inextricably intertwined with the state court judgment and plaintiff had a reasonable opportunity to raise FHA defenses in the state eviction proceedings. 12(b)(1)

source_file: 9680646_2022_Williams Jr v. Heartland Realty Investors, Inc._ilnd
case_name: Andy Hope Williams, Jr., and Vonita Cruz v. Heartland Realty Investors, Inc., Heartland Willowbrook, LLC, d/b/a Willowbrook Apartment Homes, and Starr, Bejgiert, Zink, and Rowells
text: The Court granted SBZR's motion to dismiss the FDCPA claims because SBZR did not make actionable misrepresentations: Heartland Realty Investors, Inc. had authority to bring the eviction as agent for Heartland Willowbrook, LLC, the lease permitted attorney's fees for the prevailing party, the federal lawsuit did not constitute a pending eviction proceeding under Illinois law, and SBZR properly attached the required demand notice to the eviction complaint. Pro se tenants Andy Williams and Vonita Cruz sued their landlord Heartland Realty Investors and its law firm SBZR, alleging Fair Housing Act violations against the landlord and FDCPA violations against the law firm for misrepresentations in a state court eviction proceeding. The Court granted SBZR's motion to dismiss the FDCPA claims because SBZR did not violate the FDCPA—Heartland Realty had authority to pursue eviction as the landlord's agent, the lease permitted attorney's fees, and SBZR attached all required documents to the eviction complaint. Court found plaintiffs failed to state a plausible FDCPA claim because: (1) Heartland Realty Investors, Inc. had authority as agent to bring eviction; (2) lease permitted attorney's fees to prevailing party; (3) federal lawsuit is separate from state eviction proceeding; and (4) required notices were attached to complaint. All FDCPA arguments lacked factual or legal basis. 12(b)(6)

source_file: 9682870_2023_County of Cook, IL v. Wells Fargo _ Co._ilnd
case_name: County of Cook v. Wells Fargo & Co.
text: Following Seventh Circuit precedent in County of Cook v. Bank of America Corporation, the court held that the County lacked standing to bring FHA claims because the harm to individual borrowers was too remote, and the proper plaintiffs would be the borrowers themselves; accordingly, the motion to alter or amend summary judgment was denied. The County of Cook sued Wells Fargo & Co. under the Fair Housing Act alleging predatory and discriminatory lending practices ('equity stripping') targeting minority communities through loan origination, servicing, and foreclosure activities dating back to 2003. The court denied the County's motion to alter or amend summary judgment entered in Wells Fargo's favor, following Seventh Circuit precedent holding that the County lacked proximate causation because the discriminatory harm to individual borrowers was too remote to be cognizable under the FHA. The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment on alternative grounds of lack of proximate causation, holding that County of Cook lacked standing as an indirect party to bring FHA claims that could only be brought by the actual borrowers. The court found the County's claims too remote to be cognizable under the FHA. Rule 56

case_name: Norman v. Northwest Indiana CA Section 8
text: The court dismissed pro se plaintiff's Fair Housing Act complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) for failure to state a claim because she did not allege membership in a protected class or that any adverse treatment occurred because of such membership, and granted leave to amend. Pro se plaintiff LaSandra Norman, a Section 8 voucher recipient, sued her housing authority, the new owner of her rental property, and associated lenders, alleging FHA violations arising from the sale of her building and the subsequent redirection of her Housing Assistance Payments to the new owner without her consent. The court screened the complaint under the in forma pauperis statute and dismissed it for failure to state a claim, finding that the plaintiff neither identified herself as a member of a protected class nor alleged that any discrimination was based on protected-class membership. The court also found she lacked standing for her general allegations about Section 8 recipients being denied homeownership opportunities, and granted her until June 14, 2021 to file an amended complaint. Plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class under the Fair Housing Act and failed to allege facts showing discrimination based on membership in a protected class, failing to state a plausible claim for discrimination under the Iqbal/Twombly standard. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)

case_name: Lasandra Norman v. Northwest Indiana CA Section 8, et al.
text: The court denied the motion for reconsideration because the plaintiff failed to identify newly discovered evidence, an intervening change in controlling law, or a manifest legal error, and her claim—that landlord having a mortgage on a Section 8 property constitutes an FHA violation—fails to state a claim. LaSandra Norman, proceeding pro se and receiving Section 8 voucher assistance, filed a motion to enforce her right to sue under Section 813(a) of the Fair Housing Act against Northwest Indiana Community Action, apparently asserting that her landlord having a mortgage on the rental property violates the FHA. The court denied the motion, finding no basis for reconsideration under Rule 59(e) as Norman failed to identify newly discovered evidence, a change in controlling law, or manifest legal error, and her claim fails to state a valid FHA claim. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a plausible claim under the Fair Housing Act. The plaintiff's allegation that a landlord's mortgage on a Section 8 rental property constitutes discrimination does not state a cognizable FHA claim and was dismissed without prejudice initially, then with prejudice after multiple amendments. 12(b)(6) The court recognized the elements of a retaliation claim under the Fair Housing Act but found that the plaintiff failed to plausibly allege facts supporting retaliation. The complaint was dismissed for failure to state a claim under Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards. 12(b)(6)

case_name: Sandra Black v. Naomi Friedrichsen, et al.
text: The court denied defendants' motion for TRO and preliminary injunction to restrain plaintiff from social media posts because the requested injunctive relief has no relation to the merits judgment defendants seek, defendants have adequate remedies at law through protective orders and discovery sanctions, and First Amendment concerns and public interest in open litigation outweigh any reputational harm. Sandra Black, a pro se litigant, sued Naomi Friedrichsen and others under the Fair Housing Act; this opinion addresses defendants' motion for a TRO/preliminary injunction to restrain Black from posting about the case on social media and for sanctions. The court denied the motion, finding the requested injunction improper because it lacks connection to the merits, adequate legal remedies exist, and First Amendment interests outweigh the defendants' reputational concerns. The court denied the defendants' motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction seeking to enjoin the plaintiff from posting social media comments, finding that such an injunction would not preserve the relative positions of the parties pending trial on the merits of the underlying Fair Housing Act claims, and that reputational harm did not outweigh the plaintiff's First Amendment interests and the public interest in open litigation. The court noted that alternative remedies under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (protective orders, discovery sanctions) were available. Motion for TRO and Preliminary Injunction Denied

case_name: Shedrick Northern v. Pedcor Management Corp., et al.
text: The court struck plaintiff's emergency amended complaint because he failed to first move to vacate the judgment under Rules 59(e) or 60(b) before seeking to amend after judgment was entered. Pro se plaintiff Shedrick Northern filed suit against Pedcor Management Corp. alleging water damage and mold from a toilet leak violated the Fair Housing Act. After the case was dismissed without prejudice for lack of federal jurisdiction, plaintiff filed an emergency amended complaint without first moving to vacate the judgment. The court struck the amended complaint as procedurally improper because plaintiff failed to comply with the requirement to first set aside the judgment under Rules 59(e) or 60(b) before seeking amendment post-judgment. The court found the claim was a typical state court landlord-tenant dispute that did not invoke federal jurisdiction or provisions of the Fair Housing Act. Judge Simon dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening, finding the claim lacked a federal question and belonged in state court. Dismissed without prejudice for lack of jurisdiction

case_name: Mabry v. City of East Chicago
text: The court granted plaintiffs' motion to retax costs and vacated the clerk's taxation of $13,620.98 in costs, finding that plaintiffs are indigent and cannot pay, litigated in good faith, and defendants did not oppose the waiver request. Plaintiffs Kendra Mabry and Angela Espinoza, who lost at summary judgment on their Fair Housing Act claims regarding housing conditions at a residential complex with lead and arsenic contamination, filed a motion to retax costs seeking waiver of $13,620.98 in costs imposed against them. The court granted the motion, finding plaintiffs indigent, litigated in good faith, and unable to pay without severe impact on their families and housing stability. Judgment was entered in favor of Defendants on December 28, 2023. The Fair Housing Act and equal protection claims were decided on summary judgment and resulted in a loss for Plaintiffs, though the opinion does not detail the substantive legal analysis of the FHA claims themselves—this opinion addresses only the post-judgment motion to waive costs. Rule 56

case_name: Ronnie Joe Forte v. Hopkinsville Housing Authority et al.
text: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim for failure to state a claim because the FHA does not prohibit discrimination based on criminal history, and federal law expressly permits public housing agencies to deny admission to federally assisted housing for drug-related criminal activity. Pro se plaintiff Ronnie Joe Forte sued the Hopkinsville Housing Authority and a Section 8 housing specialist under the FHA after his housing application was denied based on a blanket ban tied to his pending drug-related criminal charges. Conducting mandatory § 1915(e)(2) screening, the court found that the FHA does not cover discrimination based on criminal history and that 42 U.S.C. § 13661(c) expressly authorizes housing authorities to deny admission to applicants engaged in drug-related criminal activity. The lawsuit was dismissed for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted. The FHA does not prohibit discrimination based on criminal history. Plaintiff alleged denial based on pending drug-related criminal charges, which is not a protected class under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a) (race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin). Additionally, 42 U.S.C. § 13661(c) explicitly permits public housing agencies to deny admission based on drug-related criminal activity. Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)

case_name: Cheryl L. Fenelon et al. v. U.S. Dept. of Housing & Urban Development et al.
text: The court declined to rule on the TRO and instead granted plaintiffs leave to amend their complaint because the complaint failed to allege sufficient facts to establish subject matter jurisdiction. Pro se plaintiffs Cheryl Fenelon and Barbara Jackson filed a vague complaint against HUD, DOJ, and 19 other defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations and seeking emergency injunctive relief, but the complaint contained only four sentences with no factual allegations and failed to establish subject matter jurisdiction. The court declined to rule on the TRO and granted plaintiffs until August 8, 2021, to amend their complaint to state a valid basis for jurisdiction. Court found no factual allegations regarding FHA violations and could not determine subject matter jurisdiction. Plaintiffs granted leave to amend complaint by August 8, 2021, to state a valid basis for jurisdiction before court would rule on TRO or proceed further. 12(b)(1)

case_name: Cheryl L Fenelon et al v. U.S. Dept of Housing & Urban Development et al
text: The court dismissed the case without prejudice for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the pro se plaintiffs' complaint contained no factual allegations supporting jurisdiction under the Fair Housing Act or any other cited statute. Pro se plaintiffs Cheryl Fenelon and Barbara Jackson filed a four-sentence complaint against 21 defendants—including federal agencies, federal judges, and private entities—citing Fair Housing Act violations, conspiracy to violate civil rights, and antitrust violations, but included no factual allegations describing how any statute was violated or what any defendant did. The court twice extended deadlines for plaintiffs to amend and cure the jurisdictional deficiency, but plaintiffs refused to amend and failed to comply by the final deadline. Accordingly, the court dismissed the matter without prejudice for failure to establish subject matter jurisdiction. The complaint asserts FHA violations but contains only four sentences with no factual allegations describing how the FHA was violated, what relief is sought, or how any defendant is connected to the alleged violations. The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiffs failed to plead facts establishing jurisdiction despite two opportunities to amend. 12(b)(1)

case_name: Dawn Thompson v. Evolve Bank & Trust and PennyMac Loan Services, LLC
text: The court denied plaintiff's motion to remand, holding that PennyMac's pre-service removal was procedurally proper because service is not a prerequisite for removal under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b), and that federal question jurisdiction existed based on the multiple federal law claims alleged in the complaint. Pro se plaintiff Dawn Thompson sued her mortgagee Evolve Bank & Trust and mortgage servicer PennyMac Loan Services in Worcester County Superior Court, alleging eleven counts of federal and state law violations arising from the origination of her mortgage and the subsequent sale of her Worcester, Massachusetts property. PennyMac removed the action to federal court before either defendant had been served, prompting Thompson to move for remand on the grounds that pre-service removal was procedurally improper. The court denied remand, relying on First Circuit precedent establishing that service is generally not a prerequisite for removal and finding that federal question jurisdiction was plainly established by Thompson's federal claims under the 14th Amendment, ECOA, 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982, FHA regulations, CARES Act, and the ADA. The court found subject matter jurisdiction existed under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 because the complaint alleged multiple federal law violations (14th Amendment, ECOA, Fair Housing Act regulations, CARES Act, ADA), and supplemental jurisdiction applied to state law claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1367. Removal was proper and timely under Novak v. Bank of N.Y. Mellon Trust Co., which permits pre-service removal. The motion to remand was denied. Motion to Remand Denied

case_name: Dollie Truesdale v. Isabel Mercedes Cumming, et al.
text: The court dismissed the action for lack of standing because plaintiff failed to allege a causal connection between the named defendants (city inspectors and solicitors) and the injuries she suffered from water billing and property sales — the officials were not responsible for installing water meters, placing liens, or selling properties. Pro se plaintiff Dollie Truesdale sued Baltimore City Inspector General and City Solicitor officials alleging Fair Housing Act and Civil Rights Act claims challenging disparities in water billing and property lien sales compared to Baltimore County. The court dismissed the action for lack of standing because the named defendants were not causally connected to the injuries alleged — they neither caused the water billing practices nor ordered the property sales. Plaintiff lacks standing because the conduct she contests (water billing and property sales) is not fairly traceable to the named defendants (Inspector General, City Solicitor, and special agent). The defendants allegedly declined to investigate but did not cause the underlying injuries. The court alternatively granted the motion under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a plausible claim. 12(b)(1) and 12(b)(6)

case_name: Smith v. New Rez, LLC
text: The court dismissed all federal claims (FHA, ECOA, TILA) as barred by res judicata because plaintiff had a full and fair opportunity to raise these claims in the prior state foreclosure proceedings that reached a final judgment. Pro se plaintiff Kendall Smith sued mortgage servicer Shellpoint and property purchaser North Star following foreclosure on his Hyattsville, Maryland home, alleging violations of the FHA, ECOA, and TILA based on discriminatory lending and wrongful eviction. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding all claims barred by res judicata because the same parties, claims, and final judgment existed in the prior state foreclosure action. All claims are barred by the doctrine of res judicata because they involve the same parties or their privies, arise from the same nucleus of facts as the state foreclosure action, and could have been raised in the original state court proceedings, which reached final judgment on the merits through ratification of sale. 12(b)(1) / Res Judicata

case_name: Tamara Johnson, et al. v. The City of Annapolis, et al.
text: Court granted limited discovery to allow the City to depose plaintiffs' expert Dr. Parnell and receive Ms. Holliday's interrogatory responses, but denied broader discovery requests as the City failed to identify specific withheld information that would create a genuine dispute of material fact. Tamara Johnson and other tenants sued the City of Annapolis alleging the City's non-inspection housing policy produced a disparate impact on protected classes; the City moved for additional discovery under Rule 56(d) and for an extension to respond to plaintiffs' partial summary judgment motion. The court granted limited discovery to permit the City to depose plaintiffs' expert and obtain interrogatory responses, but denied the broader discovery request as too general, and gave the City 30 additional days to respond to the summary judgment motion. The court granted in part the City's Rule 56(d) motion to allow further discovery (expert deposition and interrogatory responses) before ruling on the plaintiffs' partial motion for summary judgment on disparate impact liability. The merits of the disparate impact claim have not yet been decided; the opinion addresses only discovery and scheduling issues. Rule 56(d) — Further Discovery Ordered

source_file: 9741834_2023_National Fair Housing Alliance v. Bank of America, National Association_mdd
case_name: National Fair Housing Alliance v. Bank of America, National Association
text: The court adopted a hybrid discovery approach requiring Phase III discovery on six cities with subsequent dispositive motions practice, while also ordering defendants to begin preparing property-level documents for Phase IV; redaction of personal identifying information is not required except for Maryland customers under state financial privacy law. National Fair Housing Alliance and companion organizations sued Bank of America alleging the bank engaged in discriminatory maintenance and marketing of bank-owned properties across 37 cities, potentially on a discriminatory basis related to race or national origin. This court order resolves a discovery dispute by adopting a phased discovery approach and determining redaction requirements under state financial privacy laws. Court denied defendants' summary judgment motions on disparate impact claim, finding that steps two and three of the Fair Housing Act's disparate impact framework had not yet been fully explored through discovery, and that subsequent motions for summary judgment on remaining issues are appropriate. Rule 56

source_file: 9741918_2023_Estate of DaMon R. Fisher v. City of Annapolis_mdd
