case_name: Tamara Johnson, et al. v. The City of Annapolis, et al. / The Estate of Damon R. Fisher, et al. v. The City of Annapolis, et al.
text: The court granted in part the City's Rule 56(d) motion, allowing limited discovery (deposition of plaintiffs' expert Dr. Parnell and interrogatory answers from Ms. Holliday) but denied the motion as to other unspecified grounds, and extended the deadline to respond to partial summary judgment by 30 days. In consolidated cases, Black renters and the Estate of Damon Fisher sued the City of Annapolis alleging the City's non-inspection policy for rental housing disproportionately impacts Black renters in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court granted in part the City's Rule 56(d) motion for additional discovery, allowing the City to depose plaintiffs' expert Dr. Parnell and obtain Ms. Holliday's interrogatory answers, but denied the motion as to other unspecified discovery requests, and gave the City 30 additional days to respond to plaintiffs' partial summary judgment motion. The court granted in part the City's Rule 56(d) motion for further discovery, allowing the City to depose the plaintiffs' expert Dr. Parnell and obtain interrogatory responses from class representative Ms. Holliday before ruling on the plaintiffs' partial motion for summary judgment on disparate impact liability. The merits of the disparate impact claim have not yet been decided. Rule 56(d) Motion

source_file: 9742608_2023_CASA de Maryland, Inc. v. Arbor Realty Trust, Inc._mdd
case_name: CASA de Maryland, Inc. v. Arbor Realty Trust, Inc.
text: The court granted preliminary approval of the $3,000,000 settlement fund, finding the settlement terms fair, reasonable, and adequate in comparison to potential per-apartment damages of $18,798 per year under Maryland law, given the risks of litigation and the strength of the case. CASA de Maryland and individual tenants sued Arbor Realty Trust and related entities alleging that Defendants failed to maintain and repair Bedford and Victoria Station apartment complexes, and discriminated against tenants through deficient housing conditions in violation of the Fair Housing Act, Prince George's County Code, and Maryland common law. The court granted preliminary approval of a $3,000,000 class settlement, finding the settlement terms fair and adequate given the $18,798 potential per-year recovery at trial versus the estimated average recovery of $4,750 per year under the settlement, and certified the settlement class of approximately 2,356 current and former tenants. Plaintiffs alleged Fair Housing Act violations based on discriminatory failure to maintain and repair properties. The case was resolved by settlement agreement with a $3,000,000 Settlement Fund, preliminarily approved as fair, reasonable, and adequate under Fed.R.Civ.P. 23(e). The court did not reach the merits of the FHA claims, as the parties resolved the dispute through negotiated settlement. Settlement Agreement Plaintiffs alleged violations of Prince George's County Code § 13-153 and Maryland common law (breach of contract and breach of implied warranty of habitability) based on deficient maintenance and repair. These claims were resolved by the same settlement agreement, with damages measured under Maryland law as the difference between rent paid and reasonable rental value of the unit in its condition. Settlement Agreement

source_file: 9743469_2024_Clark v. Council of Unit Owners of the 100 Harborview Drive Condominium_mdd
case_name: Dr. Paul C. Clark, Sr., et al. v. Council of Unit Owners of the 100 Harborview Drive Condominium Association
text: The court granted in part and denied in part Plaintiffs' Motion for Reconsideration, ordering Defendant to search current Board Members' private email accounts for any responsive communications to John Cochran from 2019-21 regarding Plaintiffs, while also requiring production of documents the court determined were not protected by attorney-client privilege or work product. Dr. Paul Clark and family sued the 100 Harborview Drive Condominium Association alleging the HOA retaliated against them for exercising Fair Housing Act rights in connection with disputes over unit conditions and remediation. This opinion addresses discovery disputes regarding search of Board Members' private email accounts and sufficiency of Defendant's privilege log. The court ordered Defendant to conduct a limited search of current Board Members' private emails for responsive communications and to produce documents the court found were not protected by attorney-client privilege or work product. This is a discovery dispute regarding email production and privilege log sufficiency in a retaliation case that survived a motion to dismiss. The court has not reached the merits of the retaliation claim itself; it is managing discovery to develop the factual record. The case remains pending on the underlying FHA retaliation allegations. Motion for Reconsideration (Discovery Dispute)

case_name: In re: William A. Rankin and Shirley A. Rankin v. Brian Lavan and Associates, P.C.
text: The court denied debtor's motion for reconsideration and motion for summary judgment, finding no palpable defect in the magistrate's recommendation to deny reopening the bankruptcy case under Rule 60(d)(3), and that the FHA claims raised were not properly before the court in a Rule 60 motion. Debtors/Appellants William and Shirley Rankin filed motions for reconsideration and summary judgment in their long-pending bankruptcy case, seeking to reopen proceedings under Rule 60(d)(3) based on alleged fraud on the bankruptcy court, while also raising Fair Housing Act claims. The district court denied both motions, finding the motions untimely and that debtors failed to demonstrate fraud on the court sufficient to warrant relief. The court determined that new causes of action, including FHA claims, were not properly before the court in a Rule 60(d)(3) motion for relief from a judgment concerning underlying bankruptcy proceedings. The court found that objections to a Report and Recommendation are not an appropriate avenue to bring new claims or motions, and that such claims were barred by collateral estoppel as previously adjudicated in appellate review. Rule 60(d)(3) motion to reopen denied

case_name: Channel E. Allen v. Michigan First Credit Union
text: The court accepted the magistrate judge's report and denied the motion to dismiss as moot because the parties agreed to substitute Michigan First Credit Union as the proper defendant. Pro se plaintiff Channel E. Allen filed a Fair Housing Act lawsuit against the wrong entity; the parties agreed to substitute Michigan First Credit Union as the proper defendant. The court accepted the magistrate judge's recommendation and denied the pending motion to dismiss as moot.

case_name: David Roy Worthy v. Community Management Associates, Inc.
text: Plaintiff's FHA and § 1983 discrimination claims based on denial of a Section 8 housing voucher due to criminal history fail to state a claim because criminal history is not a protected class under the Fair Housing Act and individuals with criminal convictions do not constitute a suspect class for Equal Protection purposes. Pro se plaintiff David Worthy sued Community Management Associates, a Section 8 housing administrator, after his housing choice voucher application was denied based on past criminal activity, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 1983. The court granted IFP status but dismissed the complaint with prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii), holding that criminal history is not a protected characteristic under the FHA's enumerated categories and that persons convicted of crimes are not a suspect class under the Equal Protection Clause. The court further noted that federal regulations not only permit but in certain cases require housing authorities to deny voucher program admission based on criminal history. Criminal history is not a protected class under the Fair Housing Act, and federal law expressly authorizes housing authorities to deny admission based on criminal activity. The complaint fails to state a plausible discrimination claim. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) Individuals convicted of crimes do not constitute a suspect class for equal protection purposes, and federal law expressly authorizes housing authorities to consider criminal history in determining eligibility for public housing programs. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)

source_file: 9755770_2024_Johnson Chambers v. Michigan First Credit Union_mied
case_name: Yolanda Johnson Chambers v. Michigan First Credit Union
text: Chambers' FHA claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604 is time-barred because the mortgage was acquired in 2011 and the claim was brought in 2023, exceeding the FHA's two-year statute of limitations. Pro se plaintiff Yolanda Johnson Chambers, individually and as personal representative of her deceased husband's estate, sued Michigan First Credit Union and other defendants alleging that foreclosure of her home violated the Fair Housing Act and other federal and state laws. The court dismissed her federal claims, including the FHA claim as time-barred because the mortgage was acquired in 2011 and the 2023 filing exceeded the two-year statute of limitations, and remanded state law claims to Wayne County Circuit Court. The court held that plaintiff's FHA claim under § 3604 (relating to acquiring a home) was time-barred under the FHA's two-year statute of limitations because the subject property was purchased in 2011 and the claim was brought in 2023. The court found that defendants' post-2018 actions had nothing to do with the acquisition of the home. 12(b)(6) / Statute of Limitations

case_name: Robert Servis, Jr., et al. v. Inyoung Jang, et al.
text: Plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claims were dismissed because the complaint failed to identify what provision of the FHA Defendants allegedly violated or allege sufficient facts to support a claim, and alternatively because the claims were barred by res judicata from a prior state court judgment. Tenants Robert Servis, Jr. and others sued landlords Inyoung Jang and others asserting Fair Housing Act violations arising from a landlord-tenant dispute where tenants took possession of a rental house without signing a lease and stopped paying rent. The court dismissed the FHA claims for failure to state a claim because plaintiffs failed to identify which FHA provision was violated or plead sufficient factual allegations, and alternatively found the claims barred by res judicata from prior state court litigation. Court dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly because plaintiffs alleged only conclusory assertions of discrimination without identifying any FHA provision violated or providing factual allegations supporting any cognizable theory. Court also held claims were barred by res judicata as alternative ground. 12(b)(6)

source_file: 9775981_2022_Auburn Hills Homeowners Association v. New Page Properties, L.L.C._mowd
case_name: Auburn Hills Homeowners Association v. New Page Properties, L.L.C.
text: The HOA lacks standing to bring FHA claims as it is not an 'aggrieved person' under § 3613(a)(1), and federal question jurisdiction does not exist where the FHA appears only as a potential defense to the HOA's state law breach of contract claim. Auburn Hills Homeowners Association filed suit seeking a declaration that its property maintenance enforcement and fines against New Page Properties do not violate the Fair Housing Act, along with a breach of contract claim. The court dismissed the case for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, holding that the HOA lacks standing to bring FHA claims and that the FHA appears only as an anticipated defense to state law claims, not as an independent basis for federal jurisdiction. The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(1). The HOA's underlying cause of action is breach of contract under state law; the Fair Housing Act appears only as an anticipated affirmative defense, which does not create federal question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331. The Declaratory Judgment Act is procedural, not jurisdictional, and cannot be used to preemptively raise a federal defense to a state law claim. 12(b)(1)

case_name: Eric Wayne Young and Wilma Jean Young v. Lake Royale Association and Lake Royale Private Company Police
text: The court dismissed plaintiffs' claims for retaliation in violation of the Fair Housing Act under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 for failure to state a claim, adopting the magistrate judge's recommendation. Eric and Wilma Young, proceeding pro se, sued Lake Royale Association and related entities asserting Fair Housing Act retaliation claims and state law claims arising from disputes regarding property access and association enforcement. The court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation to dismiss the FHA retaliation claims for failure to state a claim and declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims. The magistrate judge recommended dismissal of the retaliation claim under § 3617 for failure to state a claim under the Iqbal/Twombly plausibility standard. The district court adopted this recommendation without clear error, finding the magistrate judge's analysis thorough. 12(b)(6) The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1367, resulting in dismissal of those claims. Supplemental jurisdiction declined under 28 U.S.C. § 1367

case_name: Gerald Thomas Mescall v. Renaissance at Antiquity, et al.
text: Court granted pro se plaintiff leave to amend complaint after finding the original complaint 'hardly a model of clarity or brevity' and administratively denied the pending motions to dismiss without prejudice to refile after amended complaint is filed Pro se plaintiff Gerald Thomas Mescall, representing himself and fourteen other senior citizens, sued Renaissance at Antiquity apartment complex and others alleging 'elder abuse' including faulty elevators, access issues, and unlawful rental rate increases under the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Older Americans Act. The court denied the pending motions to dismiss as moot and granted plaintiff leave to amend his complaint by December 15, 2023, finding the original complaint lacked clarity and organization. Court granted pro se plaintiff leave to amend complaint before ruling on motion to dismiss, finding that factual allegations, if fully developed, could possibly give rise to actionable claims. Motions to dismiss were denied as moot without prejudice to refile after amended complaint. Motion to Dismiss Denied as Moot; Leave to Amend Granted Court granted pro se plaintiff leave to amend complaint before ruling on motion to dismiss. Non-FHA claims survive procedural challenge and remain pending pending filing of amended complaint. Motion to Dismiss Denied as Moot; Leave to Amend Granted

case_name: Phyllis M. Knight v. John C. Chatelain
text: The court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because Knight's claims seek review of state court eviction judgments, and the FHA claim is not analyzed substantively. Phyllis M. Knight sued John C. Chatelain, an attorney, seeking damages related to an eviction from residential property in Omaha, Nebraska, citing the Fair Housing Act among other federal statutes. The court dismissed the case without prejudice for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, holding that Knight was effectively seeking review of state court eviction judgments and that any FHA claim was not substantively analyzed. The court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because the complaint challenged a state-court eviction judgment rendered before the federal proceeding commenced. The court noted that a state-court loss cannot be the basis for a federal FHA retaliation claim based on the same eviction. Dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under Rooker-Feldman doctrine

case_name: Knight v. Biggs
text: The court dismissed Knight's pro se complaint, finding her § 1983 conspiracy claim failed because she only made conclusory allegations without specific facts showing a meeting of the minds, and her references to constitutional provisions and federal statutes including the Fair Housing Act did not state viable claims against a private citizen. Phyllis Knight, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, sued Earl Biggs Jr. alleging constitutional violations, RICO violations, and Fair Housing Act claims arising from her eviction from a residential property in Omaha, Nebraska. The District Court dismissed Knight's complaint without prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2), finding she failed to state plausible claims because her § 1983 conspiracy allegations were conclusory, her constitutional references did not establish valid causes of action, and Biggs as a private citizen was not subject to suit under the cited federal statutes. Court dismissed all claims as frivolous or failing to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B) screening. Plaintiff alleged violations of RICO, § 1983 conspiracy, First Amendment religious liberty, Supremacy Clause, Commerce Clause, ADA, RFRA, Title VII, 18 U.S.C. § 247, 15 U.S.C. § 45, and Indian Treaties. The court found: (1) § 1983 conspiracy claim lacks specific factual allegations of a 'meeting of the minds' between Biggs and state officials; (2) religious liberty claim fails because eviction was based on rent arrears, not religious practice; (3) Supremacy Clause does not create independent private right of action; (4) Commerce Clause claim lacks factual allegations of violation; (5) RICO claim fails to allege required elements of enterprise, pattern, and racketeering activity; (6) other statutes cited (FTC Act, ADA, RFRA, Title VII, § 247) do not give rise to claims on facts alleged; (7) treaty references are frivolous. The Fair Housing Act was cited in the complaint but no FHA-specific claim was analyzed or addressed on the merits. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)

case_name: AB Realty, LLC v. Lane
text: The court granted plaintiffs leave to amend finding the proposed amendments were not futile and defendants would not be prejudiced, declining to reach the merits of any claims at the amendment stage. Plaintiffs AB Realty LLC, Kay Anderson, and Janae Anderson sought leave to amend their complaint against Scott Lane and others to preserve claims and remedy deficiencies identified in a prior dismissal order. The court granted the motion, finding the proposed amendments were not futile and defendants would not be prejudiced by allowing amendment, with the court declining to evaluate the merits of the claims at this procedural stage. The court granted plaintiffs' motion for leave to amend the complaint, finding it was not futile and that the disparate treatment FHA claim should be determined on the merits rather than dismissed at the pleading stage. The claim survives the procedural challenge and remains pending pending resolution of state criminal proceedings. Motion to Amend Granted

case_name: Michael A. D'Antonio v. Borough of Allendale, et al.
text: Motion for reconsideration denied where plaintiff failed to identify intervening change in law, new evidence, or clear error of law, and merely attempted to relitigate previously rejected arguments regarding standing and preclusion of his FHA claims. Michael D'Antonio, a developer, sued the Borough of Allendale and other defendants alleging they interfered with his attempts to build affordable housing on a property and ultimately evicted him, asserting claims including under the Fair Housing Act. The Court denied D'Antonio's motion for reconsideration of the dismissal of his Third Amended Complaint, finding he lacked standing to bring claims on behalf of a corporation, his claims were precluded, and he failed to state a viable claim. Plaintiff lacked standing because the Subject Property was owned by Calm Corporation, not Plaintiff himself, and a corporation must bring suit on its own behalf. Additionally, Plaintiff was precluded from bringing claims already fully litigated under Rooker-Feldman, Entire Controversy, Res Judicata, and Collateral Estoppel doctrines, and failed to state a claim under Rule 8 and 9. 12(b)(6) and standing/preclusion

source_file: 9811823_2024_FRANKLIN v. THE JERSEY CITY HOUSING AUTHORITY_njd
case_name: Edwina Franklin v. The Jersey City Housing Authority, Secretary, Department of Housing and Urban Development
text: The court dismissed Plaintiff's motion for default judgment without prejudice because after filing the Consolidated and Amended Complaint, Plaintiff failed to obtain a new entry of default under Rule 55(a) before moving for default judgment. Pro se Plaintiff Edwina Franklin filed a second motion for default judgment against the Jersey City Housing Authority and HUD, alleging Fair Housing Act and Equal Credit Opportunity Act violations in connection with her public housing. The court dismissed the motion without prejudice on procedural grounds, holding that because Plaintiff filed a Consolidated and Amended Complaint after the original default was entered, she was required to obtain a new entry of default before moving for default judgment under Rule 55. The court dismissed the motion for default judgment without prejudice because plaintiff failed to obtain a new entry of default under Rule 55(a) after filing the Consolidated and Amended Complaint. The procedural defect prevented the court from reaching the merits of the underlying FHA claims. Rule 55(b)(2) — Motion for Default Judgment

case_name: Ronnie J. Thomas v. Linda Bridge, Thea Guerin, and Esther Lucero
text: Complaint dismissed without prejudice for failure to state a claim, but plaintiff granted leave to amend within 21 days because it is not obvious amendment would be futile Pro se plaintiff Ronnie Thomas sued officials of the Albuquerque Housing Authority alleging Fair Housing Act, due process, and equal protection violations related to his Section 8 voucher application and waiting list position. The Court granted in forma pauperis status but dismissed the complaint for failure to state any cognizable claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, finding no factual allegations establishing a protected property interest in a not-yet-awarded voucher or demonstrating how defendants treated him differently from others similarly situated. The court found that plaintiff's conclusory allegations regarding Section 8 policies, due process violations, and equal protection violations failed to state a claim under § 1983 because they lacked factual allegations identifying specific policies, showing a protected property interest in an unawarded voucher, or demonstrating personal responsibility of each defendant for differential treatment. However, the court determined it was not obvious that amendment would be futile and granted leave to file an amended complaint. Failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)

case_name: Ronnie J. Thomas v. Linda Bridge, Thea Guerin, and Esther Lucero
text: The complaint fails to state a claim under § 1983 because plaintiff made only conclusory allegations that defendants failed to follow Section 8 policies without identifying which specific policies were violated or how they created a federal right. Pro se plaintiff Ronnie J. Thomas sued three Albuquerque Housing Authority Section 8 officials under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, due process, and equal protection related to his Section 8 voucher application and complaints about the waiting list process. The court dismissed the case without prejudice because the complaint failed to state a claim upon which relief can be granted and plaintiff failed to file an amended complaint as ordered by the magistrate judge. The court found that plaintiff's conclusory allegations that defendants failed to follow Section 8 policies were insufficient to state a claim under § 1983 because there were no factual allegations identifying the specific policies or showing they created a federal right. The complaint also failed to allege facts showing plaintiff possessed a protected property interest in an unawarded voucher or that defendants violated procedural due process or equal protection by treating plaintiff differently from similarly situated persons. 12(b)(6)

case_name: Victoria-Joy Godwin v. Senior Garden Apartments, et al.
text: The court granted all five unopposed motions to dismiss under Local Rule 7-2(d), which treats a party's failure to file a response as consent to granting the motion, dismissing all claims against all named defendants. Pro se plaintiff Victoria-Joy Godwin filed a fourth amended complaint against Senior Garden Apartments and numerous defendants—including state court judges and court personnel—alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, operation of a racketeering scheme, and civil conspiracy using state court personnel to intimidate her. Defendants filed five motions to dismiss, none of which plaintiff opposed. The court dismissed all claims on procedural grounds under Local Rule 7-2(d) and also granted a motion to strike plaintiff's improper request for judicial notice. All FHA claims against all defendants were dismissed pursuant to unopposed motions to dismiss under Local Rule 7-2(d), which treats failure to file a response as consent to granting the motion. The court did not reach the merits of any specific FHA claim. 12(b)(6) All non-FHA claims (RICO, civil conspiracy) were dismissed as unopposed motions to dismiss. The court did not engage substantively with the elements of these claims. 12(b)(6)

case_name: Jean Robert Saint-Jean, et al. v. Emigrant Mortgage Company, et al.
text: The court denied plaintiff's motion for entry of judgment on her TILA claim, finding that TILA's material disclosure requirements are evaluated based on the terms of the loan agreement at the time of closing, not on the borrower's subsequent actual performance; therefore, even though the loan later defaulted, the original disclosures accurately reflected the contractual payment schedule. Jean Robert and Edith Saint-Jean sued Emigrant Mortgage Company alleging violations of TILA, the Fair Housing Act, ECOA, and state and city human rights laws arising from a mortgage loan. This opinion addresses only Edith Saint-Jean's motion for entry of judgment on her TILA claim, which the court denied because the TIL disclosure accurately reflected the contractual loan terms at closing, and any inaccuracies from the borrower's subsequent default did not violate TILA's disclosure requirements. The court concluded that the TIL Disclosure accurately reflected the terms of the legal obligation at the time of closing and that post-closing inaccuracies resulting from the borrowers' default do not violate TILA's material disclosure requirements under 12 C.F.R. § 226.17(e). The court rejected plaintiff's argument that Emigrant should have anticipated default and adjusted disclosures accordingly, finding that such anticipatory estimation would frustrate TILA's disclosure purposes. Motion for Entry of Judgment Denied

source_file: 9847385_2021_Cedar Development East,LLC v. Town Board of Hurley_nynd
case_name: Cedar Development East, LLC v. Town Board of Hurley
text: The court denied plaintiff's motion to remand, finding defendants' removal was timely, all remaining defendants properly consented, any procedural defects in removing documents were curable and non-jurisdictional, defendants did not waive removal by requesting an extension, and the court has supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining federal constitutional and statutory claims. Cedar Development East, LLC sued the Town Board of Hurley and related defendants in state court challenging Local Law 4, a zoning ordinance limiting multi-family housing to four units and prohibiting housing in buildings exceeding 120 feet, alleging it violated the Fair Housing Act and Equal Protection Clause. The court denied plaintiff's motion to remand, ruling that removal was timely, defendants properly consented, any procedural defects were curable, and the court has supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining federal claims.

case_name: United States of America v. Douglas Waterbury, et al.
text: The court found clear and convincing evidence that defendants violated the consent decree by failing to relinquish control of the Morrisville property for approximately seven months and by continuing property management involvement in Oswego properties after the independent management agreement took effect, warranting $15,000 in sanctions but denying additional injunctive relief. The United States moved for contempt against Douglas and Carol Waterbury for allegedly violating a 2019 consent decree requiring them to hire an independent property manager and cease property management activities at their rental properties. The court found defendants in contempt for failing to relinquish control of the Morrisville property and for continued management involvement in Oswego properties, imposing $15,000 in sanctions and requiring detailed accounting. The court found clear and convincing evidence that defendants violated the Consent Decree by failing to relinquish control of rental properties to the Independent Manager, continuing to engage in property management activities, and allowing Douglas Waterbury to enter properties and contact tenants in violation of explicit prohibitions. The court imposed $15,000 in total sanctions ($7,000 for Morrisville property violations, $3,000 for Oswego property violations, and $5,000 for Douglas Waterbury's personal violations) and ordered defendants to cease all property management responsibilities and provide detailed accountings. Contempt finding and sanctions

case_name: Tirza F. Ming v. Julia Brouillete et al.
text: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint for failure to state a claim, finding defendant Land was not a state actor for § 1983 purposes and defendant Brouillete was entitled to judicial immunity for actions taken in her judicial capacity. Pro se plaintiff Tirza F. Ming sued a private individual (Mindy A. Land) and a state Family Court Judge (Julia Brouillete) alleging civil rights violations arising from a personal living arrangement dispute and family court proceedings. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the private defendant was not a state actor for § 1983 liability and the judicial defendant was entitled to absolute judicial immunity for actions taken in her official capacity. The court dismissed claims under 42 U.S.C. § 3631 (FHA criminal provision) and 42 U.S.C. § 14141 as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2) because neither statute provides a private right of action. The court also dismissed § 1983 claims against Defendant Land for failure to allege state actor status and against Defendant Brouillete based on judicial immunity, all without substantive merits analysis. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)

case_name: Beverly Brown, et al. v. Community Preservation Partners, LLC, et al.
text: The Court grants the motion to substitute Brighid McCarthy as plaintiff because Fair Housing Act claims survive the death of a party and McCarthy, as the sole beneficiary of the deceased plaintiff's estate, is a proper successor. Plaintiffs' counsel moved to substitute Brighid McCarthy as plaintiff following the death of original plaintiff Mary Gladys Orlyk, who had been part of a Fair Housing Act lawsuit commenced in 2017. The Court granted the unopposed motion, holding that FHA claims do not extinguish upon death and McCarthy, as the sole beneficiary of Orlyk's estate, is the proper successor to continue the action.

case_name: Mohamed Samura v. Maria Figueroa; Castleton Park Management; Castleton Preservation LLC
text: The Southern District of New York transferred pro se plaintiff's FHA housing application denial claim to the Eastern District of New York because all defendants and the operative events were located in Staten Island (Richmond County), which falls within the Eastern District. Pro se plaintiff Mohamed Samura filed an FHA claim alleging defendants denied his housing application on discriminatory grounds, while defendants asserted a non-discriminatory reason—his status as a full-time student at the College of Staten Island. The Southern District of New York found venue was improper because the underlying events occurred in Staten Island and defendants' addresses were in Staten Island, both of which are in Richmond County within the Eastern District of New York. The court sua sponte transferred the action to the Eastern District of New York pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a) in the interest of justice. Court transferred case to Eastern District of New York for venue and convenience reasons under § 1404(a). The underlying events occurred in Staten Island (Eastern District), and the court found transfer appropriate in the interest of justice. No substantive FHA analysis was conducted; the case was transferred before any motion to dismiss or other merits determination. Transfer under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a)

case_name: Keisha A. Jones v. City of New York
text: The Court granted Plaintiff's request for an extension of time to file an amended complaint by December 5, 2022, without making any substantive determination on the merits of the dismissed Fair Housing Act claims. Plaintiff Keisha A. Jones, proceeding pro se, filed an action against the City of New York alleging Fair Housing Act claims that were previously dismissed for failure to state a claim. The Court now grants Plaintiff's request for an extension of time to file an amended complaint by December 5, 2022. The Court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim under the Fair Housing Act but granted Plaintiff 30 days' leave to replead. The opinion does not specify the nature of the FHA claims or the factual allegations, only that they were found insufficient under the pleading standard. 12(b)(6) The Court dismissed the § 1983 claim for failure to state a claim but granted Plaintiff leave to replead. The opinion does not detail the specific allegations or legal deficiencies. 12(b)(6)

case_name: Keisha A. Jones v. City of New York, et al.
text: The Court granted Plaintiff's request for a 30-day extension of time to file an amended complaint, warning that failure to comply will result in entry of judgment consistent with the prior dismissal order. Pro se Plaintiff Keisha A. Jones, who was previously granted leave to replead claims under the Fair Housing Act following dismissal for failure to state a claim, requested an extension of the filing deadline due to illness; the Court granted the extension allowing Plaintiff until December 15, 2022, to submit an amended complaint. The Court dismissed the original complaint for failure to state a claim under the Fair Housing Act but granted Plaintiff 30 days' leave to replead. The opinion does not specify the nature of the FHA claims or the factual allegations, as it addresses only a procedural extension request following the initial dismissal order. 12(b)(6)

case_name: Harold Warren, MD v. 111 Tenants Corporation
text: The court dismissed all of plaintiff's federal claims — including FHA discrimination and retaliation, and civil rights conspiracy claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1985, and 1986 — as time-barred because the alleged conduct occurred in the 1980s and the applicable statutes of limitations had expired decades prior, and declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law claims. Pro se plaintiff Harold Warren, MD, sued 111 Tenants Corporation, a cooperative, alleging discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1985, and 1986, based on conduct the complaint itself placed in the 1980s. The court issued an order to show cause why the federal claims should not be dismissed as untimely, twice extending Warren's deadline to respond, but Warren filed no response. The court sua sponte dismissed all federal claims as untimely and declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state and city law claims. The court dismissed the FHA discrimination claim as time-barred because the conduct occurred in the 1980s and the FHA has a two-year statute of limitations under 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A), which expired decades before the 2023 filing. Statute of Limitations The court dismissed the FHA retaliation claim as time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations in 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A), as the alleged conduct occurred in the 1980s. Statute of Limitations The court dismissed all non-FHA federal claims (§§ 1981, 1982, 1985, 1986) as time-barred under their respective one to four-year limitations periods, and declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims. Statute of Limitations

case_name: Jane Doe v. Related Companies, LLP
text: The court dismissed the action without prejudice under Rule 41(b) for failure to prosecute because Plaintiff failed to respond to a show cause order within the allotted time despite receiving explicit warning that non-compliance could result in dismissal. Pro se Plaintiff Jane Doe filed a Fair Housing Act complaint against Related Companies, LLP and related defendants alleging a hostile housing environment, but the court dismissed the action without prejudice for failure to prosecute after Plaintiff ignored a show cause order directing her to explain why the complaint should not be dismissed for failing to name all parties and failing to state a plausible claim. The court dismissed the action sua sponte under Rule 41(b) for failure to prosecute after plaintiff failed to respond to a show cause order for more than six months. The court never reached the merits of any FHA claim, as dismissal was based on procedural non-compliance rather than the substantive adequacy of the allegations. Rule 41(b) dismissal for failure to prosecute

case_name: Sandra L. Cullum and Deirdre Saleh v. Wyndham Hotels & Resorts Corp., Wyndham Destinations Inc., Geoffrey A. Ballotti, Elisabeth Gale, Broadridge Corporate Issuer Solutions
text: The court granted WDI's motion to dismiss and noted the arbitration clause in the contract, granted WHR Defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction, granted Broadridge's motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim, and declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims. Plaintiffs Sandra Cullum and Deirdre Saleh sued Wyndham Hotels & Resorts Corp. and related entities alleging fraudulent inducement and deceptive practices related to a timeshare purchase made in December 2019, asserting claims under TILA, RESPA, FCRA, RICO, and other federal and state consumer protection laws. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss for failure to state valid claims and lack of personal jurisdiction, dismissed federal claims against Broadridge, and declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims, while granting plaintiffs 30 days leave to amend claims against the unserved defendant Elisabeth Gale. Plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts to state plausible claims under the various federal consumer protection statutes against the defendants. The court found that Plaintiffs' allegations were conclusory, lacked factual specificity, and did not connect the statutory requirements to the defendants' conduct. Additionally, claims against WDI were subject to mandatory arbitration under the Retail Installment Contract, and claims against WHR Defendants were dismissed for lack of personal jurisdiction. 12(b)(6), FAA arbitration, 12(b)(1) lack of subject matter jurisdiction

source_file: 9892170_2024_Tiffany Simone Fulton v. City of New York_nysd
case_name: Central Harlem Community (District 10); Silent Voices United Inc.; St. Nicholas Houses Resident Association; Tulinde LLC; Breaking the Chains of Your Mind v. City of New York; James Equities LLC; Douglas C. James; John and Jane Does
text: Artificial entities (corporations, nonprofits, and associations) cannot proceed pro se in federal court under 28 U.S.C. § 1654 and must be represented by licensed counsel, so the court directed plaintiffs to obtain legal representation within 30 days or face dismissal without prejudice. Several organizational plaintiffs — including Silent Voices United Inc., St. Nicholas Houses Resident Association, Tulinde LLC, and Breaking the Chains of Your Mind — along with Central Harlem Community District 10, filed pro se Fair Housing Act claims against the City of New York and private defendants, seeking injunctive relief and class certification. The court determined that, as artificial entities, none of the plaintiffs could proceed pro se, and that the non-lawyer individuals who signed the complaint could not represent the organizations' legal interests. The court ordered plaintiffs to retain licensed counsel by April 8, 2024, warning that failure to do so would result in dismissal without prejudice.

case_name: Tedric Kewon Jones v. Homestate Asset Management LLC
text: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because plaintiff failed to allege he was a member of any protected class (race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, or disability) or that defendant discriminated against him on the basis of a protected characteristic. Pro se plaintiff Tedric Kewon Jones sued Homestate Asset Management LLC alleging Fair Housing Act violations, claiming defendant refused to accept his Emergency Rental Assistance Program benefits, denied maintenance requests, harassed him, and attempted to evict him. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to allege membership in any protected class or facts showing discrimination based on a protected characteristic. The court dismissed the FHA claim because plaintiff failed to allege discrimination based on any protected characteristic under the FHA (race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, or disability). Plaintiff alleged only that defendant refused to accept ERAP benefits, which does not constitute FHA discrimination absent a nexus to a protected class. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) — failure to state a claim The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims and dismissed them without prejudice after dismissing the FHA claim, as there was no independent basis for federal jurisdiction. Supplemental jurisdiction declined

case_name: Chelsea Culver, et al. v. Melissa Churchill, et al.
text: The court dismissed the complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiffs failed to establish federal question jurisdiction (the FHA is irrelevant to state law eviction and defamation claims) and no diversity of citizenship exists between the Ohio parties. Pro se plaintiffs Chelsea Culver and Ben Smith sued their former landlords Melissa Churchill and Donald Zeiters in federal court, attempting to bring state law eviction and defamation claims under the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed the complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding no federal question (the FHA is irrelevant to the alleged claims) and no diversity of citizenship since all parties are Ohio residents. Court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiffs failed to allege discrimination based on any protected class under the FHA and the case involves only state law eviction and defamation claims. Neither diversity nor federal question jurisdiction exists. 12(b)(1) 28 U.S.C. § 410 provides a definition of defamation only in the context of collection of foreign defamation judgments and does not create a federal cause of action for state law defamation torts. Claim lacks federal question jurisdiction. 12(b)(1)

case_name: Ronald D. Leonard v. Amy Montgomery
text: The Magistrate Judge recommends dismissal because Younger abstention applies to ongoing state eviction proceedings, and even if the court could hear the case, plaintiff failed to state a valid § 3604 claim since he made no allegations of housing discrimination based on a protected class. Plaintiff Ronald Leonard, a tenant of the Hocking Metropolitan Housing Authority, brought suit against Office Manager Amy Montgomery alleging First Amendment retaliation and claims under 42 U.S.C. § 3604 and state law after receiving a Notice to Leave the Premises following his refusal to permit a unit inspection and his photographing of staff. The Magistrate Judge recommends dismissal under Younger abstention doctrine since state eviction proceedings are ongoing, and alternatively because plaintiff failed to state a viable claim under § 3604 as he made no allegations of discrimination based on a protected class. The court recommended dismissal under § 1915(e)(2) as frivolous and failing to state a claim. The § 1983 retaliation claim failed because plaintiff's own allegations showed the eviction was based on refusal of entry and disrespectful conduct, not protected speech. The § 3604 claim failed because plaintiff alleged no discrimination based on protected classes. State law claims were insufficiently pleaded and supplemental jurisdiction was declined. Recommended dismissal under § 1915(e)(2)

case_name: Alicia A. Epps v. Carl Linder, III, et al.
text: The motions for leave to amend and default judgment are denied as futile and premature, respectively; plaintiff's proposed amendments would not cure the duplicative nature of her complaint, and default judgment is unwarranted because defendants have not been properly served. Plaintiff Alicia A. Epps, proceeding in forma pauperis, sues former City of Cincinnati and FC Cincinnati officials and the United States, alleging Fair Housing Act and constitutional violations stemming from the demolition of public housing in Cincinnati's West End neighborhood to build a soccer stadium. The Magistrate Judge recommends denying plaintiff's motion for leave to amend her complaint as futile and her motion for default judgment as premature due to lack of proper service on defendants. Court recommended dismissal under § 1915(e)(2)(B) as frivolous and duplicative of previously litigated claims alleging FHA violations based on demolition of public housing. The complaint was deemed abusive of the judicial process because it merely repeated pending or previously litigated claims. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)

case_name: April Clark v. Blueprint Investments, LLC
text: The Court lacks subject matter jurisdiction because (1) a plaintiff cannot remove their own state court action to federal court, and (2) federal claims asserted as counterclaims do not confer federal question jurisdiction under the well-pleaded complaint rule. Plaintiff April Clark, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, attempted to remove four state court actions (including eviction proceedings) to federal court, citing the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and other federal laws as bases for jurisdiction. The Court granted in forma pauperis status but recommended remand because (1) plaintiffs cannot remove their own cases under 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a), and (2) federal counterclaims do not establish federal question jurisdiction under the well-pleaded complaint rule. The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff attempted to remove her own case from state court (which only defendants may do under § 1441) and because any federal claims were asserted as counterclaims or affirmative defenses in state court eviction proceedings, not in the plaintiff's well-pleaded complaint, and therefore could not confer original federal jurisdiction. 28 U.S.C. § 1447(d) — Remand for lack of subject matter jurisdiction

case_name: United States v. Johnson
text: Because defendant defaulted and failed to respond to the enforcement action, the court granted default judgment enforcing the conciliation agreement, awarding $5,000 in damages and requiring completion of HUD fair housing training. The United States brought this enforcement action against a private landlord for breach of conciliation agreements entered into through HUD regarding a fair housing complaint. The court granted default judgment after the defendant failed to appear or respond, awarding $5,000 in damages to the underlying complainant and ordering the defendant to complete HUD fair housing training. The United States sought enforcement of a conciliation agreement approved by HUD under 42 U.S.C. § 3610(b). After defendant's default, the court found the well-pleaded allegations established liability for breach of the conciliation agreement and entered default judgment for $5,000 in damages and an order requiring defendant to complete fair housing training. Default Judgment

case_name: Watson v. loanDepot.com, LLC
text: The court denied the motion to dismiss the Fair Housing Act claim because defendant relied on exhibits the court declined to judicially notice or incorporate by reference, but dismissed the fraud claim without prejudice for failure to adequately plead scienter. Plaintiff Nichole Watson sued loanDepot.com alleging that defendant's faulty loan origination handling ruined her pending home purchase and caused her to lose a $22,500 forgivable loan under the NeighborhoodLIFT program. The court denied the motion to dismiss the Fair Housing Act and other claims, while dismissing the fraud claim without prejudice for inadequate pleading of scienter. Court denied defendant's motion to dismiss the FHA claim because defendant relied on exhibits the court declined to judicially notice or incorporate by reference; the complaint's FHA allegations survive the motion to dismiss on pleading grounds. 12(b)(6) Court denied defendant's motion to dismiss the ECOA claim on the same basis as the FHA claim (reliance on non-judicially-noticed exhibits); fraud claim was dismissed for failure to plead knowledge element, but UTPA and OMLL claims survived because plaintiff adequately pleaded material misrepresentation or omission. 12(b)(6)

case_name: Douglas Myers et al. v. Highlands at Vista Ridge Homeowners Association, Inc. et al.
text: The court granted defendants' motion for attorney fees in the amount of $4,049.00 as a discovery sanction, rejecting plaintiffs' objections that certain time entries were redundant or should be reduced because dismissal was not granted. Plaintiffs filed this Fair Housing Act lawsuit against the Highlands at Vista Ridge Homeowners Association; the underlying claims are not described in this order, which only addresses defendants' motion for attorney fees following a discovery sanctions ruling. The court granted defendants' motion for $4,049.00 in fees, finding plaintiffs' objections to the fee amount were without merit.

case_name: Tracie Allen v. loanDepot.com, LLC
text: The court denied loanDepot's motion to dismiss plaintiff's FHA and ECOA claims, finding no clear error in the magistrate's recommendation, but granted dismissal of the fraud, UTPA, and OMLL claims for failure to adequately plead the required elements of intent and willfulness. Plaintiff Tracie Allen sued mortgage lender loanDepot.com, LLC alleging that a loan officer made false representations about her likelihood of loan approval and ability to meet a NeighborhoodLIFT program deadline, bringing claims under the FHA, ECOA, Oregon's Unfair Trade Practices Act, Oregon Mortgage Lender Law, and fraud. The district court adopted in part the magistrate judge's findings and recommendation, denying the motion to dismiss the FHA and ECOA claims without objection after a clear-error review, while granting dismissal of the fraud, UTPA, and OMLL claims because plaintiff failed to plausibly allege the loan officer's knowledge of falsity, reckless disregard, or willful intent at the time the statements were made. Plaintiff was granted leave to amend within thirty days. The court dismissed fraud, UTPA, and OMLL claims for failure to state a plausible claim under Iqbal/Twombly, finding that plaintiff's allegations of the loan officer's intent were conclusory and unsupported by factual allegations. The FHA and ECOA claims survived the motion to dismiss but the opinion does not substantively analyze them on the merits. 12(b)(6)

case_name: Larry Johnson v. Thomas Brenneke; Garrett Lamar Miles; Guardian Management, LLC; Guardian Real Estate Services; Uptown Tower Apartments; Lisa Simonson; Kelly Paine; and Sunshine Sales
text: The district court adopted the Magistrate Judge's Findings and Recommendation in full, denying plaintiff's partial motion for summary judgment and granting Guardian Defendants' cross-motion for summary judgment on the Fair Housing Act claims. Pro se plaintiff Larry Johnson filed a Fair Housing Act action against Guardian Management, LLC, Guardian Real Estate Services, Uptown Tower Apartments, and individual defendants alleging disability discrimination claims. The district court adopted the Magistrate Judge's Findings and Recommendation in full, denying Johnson's partial motion for summary judgment and granting Guardian Defendants' cross-motion for summary judgment. The district court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation granting Guardian Defendants' cross motion for summary judgment, finding insufficient evidence to support plaintiff's FHA claims. The court applied the summary judgment standard to the factual record and determined defendant prevailed. Rule 56

case_name: Larry Johnson v. Thomas Brenneke; Garrett Lamar Miles; Guardian Management, LLC; Guardian Real Estate Services; Uptown Tower Apartments; Lisa Simonson; Kelly Paine; and Sunshine Sales
text: This Court adopted the Magistrate Judge's Findings and Recommendation without objections, denying Plaintiff's motions for partial summary judgment, motion to amend complaint, and multiple motions for relief. Pro se Plaintiff Larry Johnson filed a Fair Housing Act action against Guardian Management, LLC and related defendants arising from housing at Uptown Tower Apartments. The Court adopted the Magistrate Judge's Findings and Recommendation in full, denying Johnson's motion for partial summary judgment, motion to amend complaint, and multiple motions for relief without conducting de novo review because no party filed objections.

case_name: Wilmore Lee Washington, III v. Farmington Estates Owners Association
text: The court adopted the F&R denying Seibel's motion to dismiss as to the disparate treatment FHA claim but granted the motion as to all other claims against her. Pro se plaintiff Wilmore Lee Washington, III sued Farmington Estates Owners Association and related parties including Natalie Seibel alleging Fair Housing Act violations. The court adopted the F&R denying Seibel's motion to dismiss as to the disparate treatment claim while granting dismissal of all other claims against her. The magistrate judge recommended denying Seibel's motion to dismiss as to the disparate treatment claim under the Fair Housing Act, finding the claim survived the motion to dismiss. The district court adopted this recommendation without objection. Motion to Dismiss The magistrate judge recommended granting Seibel's motion to dismiss as to all claims other than the disparate treatment FHA claim. The district court adopted this recommendation, dismissing all non-FHA claims against Seibel. Motion to Dismiss

source_file: 9932222_2020_GLYNN v. ELLSWORTH CONGREGATION OF LEHOVAH'S WITNESSES_paed
case_name: Glynn v. Ellsworth Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses
text: The complaint was dismissed without prejudice for failure to state a claim because it provided no factual allegations whatsoever—only biblical verses and incomprehensible demands—failing to put defendants on notice or establish any basis for federal jurisdiction. Pro se plaintiff Jermaine Glynn filed an in forma pauperis complaint against the Ellsworth Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses alleging housing discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3604, but the complaint contained only biblical scripture and incomprehensible demands without any factual allegations. The E.D. Pa. court dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) and Rule 8, granting Glynn leave to file an amended complaint. The court dismissed the complaint as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) because it failed to provide any factual allegations, failed to comply with Rule 8's pleading requirements, and was so confused and unintelligible that its true substance could not be discerned. The complaint cited § 3604 but contained no facts establishing jurisdiction, putting defendants on notice, or describing any conduct related to housing discrimination. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)

case_name: Magistrate Mahdi Sufi El v. People's Emergency Center, et al.
text: Plaintiff's retaliation claims were dismissed because claims related to the 4050 Haverford eviction were barred by the settlement agreement in El I, and Plaintiff failed to adequately plead any conspiracy or nexus between the alleged retaliatory actions and protected activity. Plaintiff, proceeding pro se, filed this action alleging retaliation under § 3617 of the Fair Housing Act against his former landlord (PEC), a housing development corporation (PHADC), and a community radio association (WPEB) for filing a previous Fair Housing Act lawsuit (El I) that was settled. The Court granted defendants' motions to dismiss because the claims regarding the eviction were barred by the settlement agreement's release, and Plaintiff failed to adequately plead any conspiracy or connection between the alleged retaliatory conduct and protected activity. Plaintiff's retaliation claim under FHA § 3617 regarding eviction from 4050 Haverford apartment was dismissed because all claims against PEC related to the eviction were waived by the settlement agreement in the prior case (El I). Claims against PHADC were dismissed for failure to plead facts showing PHADC's connection to the apartment or relationship to PEC, relying only on conclusory allegations of concerted action. 12(b)(6) Plaintiff's retaliation claim regarding eviction from LAVA space was dismissed because Plaintiff alleged only conclusory allegations of conspiracy between PEC and Winter without factual allegations showing their relationship, and failed to allege facts connecting the LAVA eviction to the protected activity in El I. 12(b)(6) Plaintiff's retaliation claim against WPEB for denial of access to radio station was dismissed because Plaintiff alleged no cause of action against WPEB in the Second Amended Complaint and offered no facts showing WPEB's relationship to any other defendant or connection to protected activity. 12(b)(6)

case_name: Geronimo F. Rosado, Jr. v. James A. Whitcraft, et al.
text: The court dismissed Rosado's Fair Housing Act claims because he failed to allege facts connecting the Defendants' actions to his membership in a protected class, as required to state a plausible FHA claim. Pro se plaintiff Geronimo Rosado sued landlord James Whitcraft and attorney Jeremiah Kane alleging Fair Housing Act violations related to an eviction dispute over rent payments and property repairs. The court dismissed Rosado's amended complaint in its entirety, finding his FHA claims failed because he did not allege facts showing discrimination based on his membership in a protected class. Plaintiff failed to allege that he was discriminated against on account of membership in a protected class. The FHA is a federal anti-discrimination statute targeting members of specific protected classes, and plaintiff's allegations concerning housing maintenance, rent increases, and eviction do not connect to any protected class status, which is fatal to any FHA claim. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) Plaintiff's allegations of harassment and intimidation do not link the alleged conduct to exercise or enjoyment of a right under the FHA or to membership in a protected class. Section 3617 prohibits acts directed at individuals 'because of' their membership in a protected class, which plaintiff failed to allege. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) Plaintiff and defendants are both citizens of Pennsylvania, so complete diversity required by 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a) does not exist. State law claims dismissed without prejudice for lack of subject matter jurisdiction; plaintiff may refile in state court. 12(b)(1) — lack of subject matter jurisdiction

source_file: 9947666_2024_Ewideh v. Homesite Insurance Company of the Midwest_pamd
case_name: Ewideh v. Homesite Insurance Company of the Midwest
text: The court transferred the case to the Middle District of Pennsylvania because a virtually identical action involving the same parties and claims was already pending there, making transfer the most efficient resolution to avoid duplicative litigation. Pro se plaintiffs Omar Ewideh and Nivertiti Geaith sued their insurer Homesite Insurance Company and its attorneys for mishandling insurance claims related to property damage at their York, Pennsylvania residence, asserting claims including breach of contract, bad faith, and Fair Housing Act violations. The court granted defendants' motion to transfer venue to the Middle District of Pennsylvania, finding that a virtually identical action between the same parties was already pending there, and the transfer would serve judicial economy by avoiding duplicative litigation. The court transferred the case to the Middle District of Pennsylvania based on Jumara factors, finding that a related pending action with nearly identical claims and parties was already filed in the Middle District, and that the plaintiffs' residence and the subject property were located in York, Pennsylvania (Middle District). The court did not reach the merits of any claim, including the FHA claim, as the case was transferred before substantive analysis. Transfer to Middle District of Pennsylvania pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a)

case_name: Lynne Thompson v. George C. Bromall, George C. Miller, Hon. Judge Chris Sherer, Leslie J. Schupp, Anthony Cimino
text: The Anti-Injunction Act precludes a federal court from enjoining state court eviction proceedings absent express congressional authorization, necessary aid of jurisdiction, or need to protect federal court judgments, and because none of these exceptions apply, the court denied Thompson's motions for injunctive relief without reaching the merits of her Fair Housing Act claims. Pro se plaintiff Lynne Thompson filed an emergency motion seeking to enjoin state court eviction proceedings, naming her landlord, his attorney, real estate agents, and the state court judge as defendants, and raising Fair Housing Act claims in addition to challenges based on the CDC COVID-19 eviction moratorium. The court denied the motions for injunctive relief, holding that the Anti-Injunction Act prohibits federal courts from enjoining state court proceedings absent applicable exceptions that do not apply in this case. The Anti-Injunction Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2283, prohibits federal court from enjoining pending state court eviction proceedings. None of the three statutory exceptions apply: (1) no clear Congressional authorization for FHA to override state court proceedings; (2) state court proceedings do not interfere with federal court jurisdiction; (3) no prior federal court judgment exists. The court did not reach the merits of the FHA or CDC moratorium claims because the Anti-Injunction Act bars the requested relief. Motion for TRO/Preliminary Injunction Denied

case_name: Cassandra McGuire v. Highmark Holdings et al.
text: The court granted McGuire's IFP application on appeal, found her proposed third amended complaint improperly filed for failure to seek leave or obtain consent, denied her frivolous defense motions and objections to the clerk's denial of default, granted her motion for extension of time to respond to discovery, and denied the defendants' motions to strike. Cassandra McGuire, proceeding pro se and IFP, sued her former employers Highmark Holdings and Enfield Management alleging she was terminated from her leasing consultant position in retaliation for reporting Fair Housing Act violations at the Nashville properties she managed. The court addressed multiple pending procedural motions, granting McGuire's IFP application on appeal and her motion for extension of time to respond to discovery, while denying her frivolous defense motions and the defendants' motions to strike. The Magistrate Judge recommended denying defendants' motion to dismiss McGuire's FHA retaliation claim, finding it survived the Rule 12(b)(6) motion. The District Court adopted this recommendation, allowing the claim to proceed to discovery. Rule 12(b)(6) The Magistrate Judge recommended dismissing McGuire's Title VII claims under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) for failure to state a claim on which relief can be granted. The District Court adopted this recommendation. The THRA retaliation claim survived and remains pending. 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii)

case_name: Samantha McDonald v. Madison Flats, et al.
text: The Magistrate Judge recommends dismissal without prejudice under Rules 4(m) and 41(b) because plaintiff failed to serve defendants with process and has had no contact with the Court since filing her lawsuit, indicating loss of interest. Pro se plaintiff Samantha McDonald filed a Fair Housing Act lawsuit against Madison Flats and Crystal Snyder alleging housing discrimination in Madison, Tennessee. The Magistrate Judge recommends dismissing the case without prejudice because plaintiff failed to serve defendants within the 90-day deadline and has had no contact with the Court since filing, constituting failure to prosecute. The action was dismissed without prejudice under Rule 4(m) for failure to serve defendants within 90 days and under Rule 41(b) for failure to prosecute, delay, and contumacious conduct. The court did not reach the merits of the FHA claims because service was never effectuated and plaintiff abandoned the action. Rule 4(m) / Rule 41(b)

case_name: Cassandra McGuire v. Highmark Holdings et al.
text: The Magistrate Judge recommends dismissing the case with prejudice under Rules 37 and 41(b) because plaintiff demonstrated bad faith and willfulness through repeated refusal to participate in discovery and continued filing of baseless default motions despite explicit warnings, but recommends denying defendants' request for attorneys' fees as unjust given plaintiff's in forma pauperis status. Cassandra McGuire, a former leasing consultant and assistant manager, sued her employer Enfield Management and related entities alleging they terminated her employment in retaliation for reporting Fair Housing Act violations. The Magistrate Judge recommends granting defendants' sanctions motion and dismissing the case with prejudice because McGuire engaged in contumacious conduct by refusing to participate in discovery, unilaterally canceling her deposition, and repeatedly filing baseless default motions despite court warnings, while recommending denial of defendants' attorneys' fees request as unjust given her in forma pauperis status. The court dismissed the action with prejudice under Rule 37 and 41(b) for plaintiff's willful failure to participate in discovery, repeated violation of court orders, and contumacious conduct, not on the merits of the retaliation claim itself. The claim was never substantively analyzed. Rule 37 and Rule 41(b) dismissal The court dismissed the action with prejudice under Rule 37 and 41(b) for plaintiff's willful failure to participate in discovery and contumacious conduct. Non-FHA claims were not separately analyzed on the merits. Rule 37 and Rule 41(b) dismissal

case_name: Larry D. Ford v. Camillo Properties, et al.
text: The court dismissed the case without prejudice solely because the pro se plaintiff failed to properly serve the defendants, making no substantive ruling on any Fair Housing Act claim. Pro se plaintiff Larry Ford sued Camillo Properties and others under the Fair Housing Act, Civil Rights Act of 1964, and other statutes, alleging harm from rental properties in his subdivision. The court dismissed the case for failure to effect proper service and denied frivolous default judgment motions, without reaching the merits. Dismissed without prejudice for failure to properly serve defendants

case_name: In re: Ditech Holding Corporation, et al.
text: The court sustained the objection and expunged the claimant's proof of claim, finding that her bare invocation of the Fair Housing Act (§ 3605) and other statutes—without any supporting factual allegations showing how Ditech discriminated or violated those statutes—failed to state a cognizable claim for relief under the Rule 12(b)(6) standard applied at the Sufficiency Hearing. Carolyn J. White filed a proof of claim in the Ditech Chapter 11 bankruptcy asserting mortgage-related grievances including PMI cancellation disputes, loan modification complaints, and short sale delays, and listed the FHA, FCRA, HAMP, and other programs as causes of action. The bankruptcy court sustained the Consumer Claims Trustee's objection and expunged the claim, finding that White's conclusory statutory citations—including her FHA reference under § 3605—were unsupported by any factual allegations sufficient to state a plausible claim. Objection sustained; claim disallowed and expunged Claim fails to state plausible FHA violation; too vague and conclusory No factual allegations supporting FCRA violation; no private right of action for furnisher violations under 15 U.S.C. § 1681s-2(a) Claims directed at prior servicer Everhome, not Ditech; HAMP program expired December 30, 2016, before claimant's May 2018 modification request Settlement distributions completed; court lacks jurisdiction; claimant makes no argument for entitlement

case_name: Dustin Barral v. Brooktree Apartments and 2300 West Apartments
text: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim because sex offender status is not a protected class under the Act, and plaintiff failed to allege membership in any protected class or that adverse actions were based on protected status. Dustin Barral, a registered sex offender, sued two Nevada apartment complexes under the Fair Housing Act after being denied housing based on a blanket policy excluding registered sex offenders. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that sex offender status is not a protected class under the FHA and plaintiff failed to state a valid discrimination claim. Dismissed without prejudice, with leave to amend Dismissed without prejudice, with leave to amend

source_file: 10841572_2026_Miguel Angel Quinones-Camacho v. Toledo Properties Owner B LLC, et al._ohnd
case_name: Miguel Angel Quinones-Camacho v. Toledo Properties Owner B LLC, et al.
text: The court abstained from exercising jurisdiction under Younger v. Harris because plaintiff has an ongoing eviction proceeding in state court, and there is no indication plaintiff is precluded from raising federal claims in that forum. Plaintiff Miguel Angel Quinones-Camacho, facing imminent eviction in Toledo Municipal Court, filed a federal action alleging defendants improperly added late fees and initiated eviction in retaliation for his request to audit documentation of those fees. case_name: Donna Mortel v. George Nowicki; Scott McClung
text: The Fifth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal for insufficient service of process under Rule 12(b)(5) and failure to prosecute under Rule 41(b), finding no abuse of discretion because Mortel failed to comply with Rule 4(e) service requirements and refused to appear at a court-ordered status conference. case_name: United States v. Texas
text: The en banc Fifth Circuit vacated the preliminary injunction against Texas S.B. 4, holding that the nonprofit plaintiff organizations and El Paso County lacked Article III standing because their alleged injuries — resource diversion and mission frustration — were voluntarily self-inflicted under FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine and did not constitute cognizable injury-in-fact. The Fifth Circuit sitting en banc vacated a district court preliminary injunction that had blocked enforcement of Texas S.B. 4, a state law criminalizing unlawful entry and reentry into Texas, because none of the plaintiffs — immigrant advocacy nonprofits and El Paso County — had Article III standing. The court held that voluntarily incurring costs to advocate for clients or adjust legal services in response to a new law does not manufacture a cognizable injury under current Supreme Court precedent. Preliminary Injunction Vacated on Standing Grounds
